- When the market is completely unaware or resistant, first eliminate three headline options: do not mention the price or any price reduction; do not put the product name in the headline or prominent display type; do not state directly what the product does, what desire it satisfies or what problem it solves. Each of these is either meaningless or will fail at that stage. [L0330.035]
- At the most unaware stage, the headline must be an identification headline. It calls the market together around an emotion, attitude or situation it already feels, sells nothing directly, and exists only to get the reader into the next paragraph. Each paragraph then pulls the reader into the next, moving from identification to awareness of the problem or desire, to the realisation that a solution exists, and finally to the product. [L0330.036]
- An identification headline must be the prospect's own headline, describing their problem and their state of mind right now. It should attract only the logical prospects and repel everyone else. It must not be a cute, funny or shocking line with no real headline behind it. [L0330.037]
- Before writing the headline, answer three questions: what mass desire drives the market, how much the market already knows about how the product satisfies it (state of awareness), and how many similar products the market has already seen (state of sophistication). The first answer gives the force. The second and third give the position of the market relative to the product and therefore the content of the headline. [L0330.017]
- A headline that works at one awareness level usually fails at another, and a headline that worked for a market will stop working once that market moves to a new level. Re-check the awareness level before reusing any headline. [L0330.019]

### Avatar document

The avatar document has six required analysis sections. Ground every claim in verbatim research data. [L0039.031, L0039.026]

| Section | What to write |
|---|---|
| (1) Awareness stage | Classify on Schwartz's 5 stages using the rule that failed-method and competitor-name language signals later stages while pure "struggling" language signals Problem-Aware, then state the copy implication. [L0039.031] |
| (2) Core fear / fear direction | The single dominant fear underneath the surface complaint, which direction it points (future dread vs. present shame), quoted from data. [L0039.031] |
| (3) Failed methods | What customers tried that didn't work, phrased as "this will never work" reasoning that copy can lean on. [L0039.031] |
| (4) Emotional drivers and trigger moments | The specific moment or circumstance that makes them buy. [L0039.031] |
| (5) Their own words | Verbatim swipe list of exact phrases customers use for the problem and desired outcome, to be echoed in copy without replacing them with marketing language. [L0039.031] |
| (6) Angle map | Distinct angles (each = fear + mechanism), ranked by data support. [L0039.031] |

- In the avatar, ground every claim about the customer in verbatim data from your research. If the research is thin on a point, state that explicitly instead of inferring or inventing customer psychology. [L0039.026]
- Give the avatar a name, an age and a photo, then write ad copy and emails as if speaking directly to that one person. A concrete, named person makes copy more specific than a broad demographic label. [L1243.014]

#### Research documentation template

```
Audience Research Documentation template: (1) List all pains and desires your audience experiences. (2) List all relevant features. (3) Define your product advantages. (4) List all problems your product solves. (5) Describe the transformation-the desired outcome and how customer life improves. Keep asking 'what does that mean?' repeatedly until you reach underlying motivations such as belonging, connection, or significance. (6) Add original angle ideas from your research.
```

[L0258.007]

- Before producing any ad creative, research the target audience's deepest needs and desires, and map how the product's features and benefits deliver that outcome. Ads that list generic benefits unrelated to the audience's needs consistently underperform. [L1348.001]

### Avatar research and buyer groups (older)

Units in this group come from the 2021-22 course and are marked older.

- Build a separate avatar for each distinct buyer group, because people with different problems, needs and buying behavior respond to different copy. A single category can often be split by experience level, for example beginner, casual and advanced buyers. (older) [L0907.009]
- Write each piece of copy for the avatar that the specific product is built for, because copy aimed at a different group will not appeal. For example, a basic entry-level running shoe should be written for first-time runners, not for marathon trainees. (older) [L0907.012]
- Record the experts, creators and personalities each avatar follows. This supports interest targeting on ad networks, since people who follow a niche expert usually share that niche's interest. (older) [L0907.014]
- Study the social profiles and content of the experts an avatar follows, and look at what their audience likes, shares and comments on. This shows the language and interests of your customer. (older) [L0907.015]
- Record the online spaces where the avatar spends time, such as Facebook groups, forums, fan pages, Reddit and Quora. Team members can read or join these spaces to learn the pains and desires of the market and to find product angles. (older) [L0907.017]
- Record the emotions the customer feels right now, such as frustration, sadness or excitement. Put yourself in their position to choose the tone for your copy. (older) [L0907.023]
- The customer avatar template comes with a filled-in example sheet. Use it to judge how much detail each field needs, but do not copy its content, because your profile must reflect your own market. (older) [L0907.030]
- A buyer of a backyard gazebo may want to host friends and be seen as a good host, so the action is entertaining guests in an outdoor space. Recording this identity and action next to the product lets copy speak to the host's goal instead of only the structure. (older) [L0907.033]
- Ads should be built around the audience. The first question is who the product is being sold to, and the message should follow from that audience's view. Custom ads should be written from this audience view. [L1187.022]

### Desires, emotions and the reason behind them

- Each desire should be paired with the emotional reason behind it, such as fear of being embarrassed, feeling unhygienic or ashamed of the home. The reason ("why") is what gives the copy its tension, so a desire without its why produces weaker messages. [L0516.002]
- Sell what the buyer wants, then deliver what they need. Buyers rarely identify their needs, but they describe their wants clearly. [L0378.074]

#### Wants and needs sort

1. Draw two columns on a sheet of paper. Label one "Wants" and the other "Needs". [L0378.073]
2. List everything the buyer says they want in the first column, and everything they actually need in the second. [L0378.073]
3. Write your sales message around the wants, then deliver the needs as the actual solution. [L0378.073]

[L0378.073]

- A strong ad angle combines three parts: a feeling the buyer has right now (for example present self-blame rather than fear of a future problem), a mechanism that explains why earlier attempts failed without blaming the buyer, and a stated reason the angle stands apart from competitors. Before using the feeling, confirm it appears across many survey responses in the buyers' own words, otherwise it is only the seller's assumption. [L1140.033]
- Competitors often speak to a symptom, such as a child's behavior. An angle about how the buyer privately judges themselves, for example feeling like they failed, can stand apart if buyers repeat that feeling in the survey. [L1140.017]

### Emotional targeting and proxy buyers

- Document each emotion's intensity on a 1-10 scale and state its duration, social dimension and who else is affected. Distinguish shame ("I am bad") from guilt ("I did something wrong"), because each drives different messaging and proxy-buyer dynamics. [L0613.028]

#### Emotional targeting matrix

Rows are customer avatars. Columns are:

| # | Column |
|---|---|
| 1 | Distress level (low, moderate, high) |
| 2 | Primary negative emotion |
| 3 | Primary positive emotion (aspiration) |

Each cell needs supporting evidence, example language and source links. [L0613.032]

#### High-stakes scenario template (build 7-10 scenarios)

1. Describe the situation in concrete detail: who is involved and what is at stake. [L0613.034]
2. Name the dominant emotion and its intensity 1-10. [L0613.034]
3. List secondary emotions and how they interact. [L0613.034]
4. Name the identity label that threatens to become permanent. [L0613.034]
5. Describe the attention state and what is being missed. [L0613.034]
6. Judge whether the scenario could trigger action. [L0613.034]
7. Write the mirror-moment reaction. [L0613.034]
8. List the permission and validation needed to allow hope. [L0613.034]
9. Describe how the scenario could become a turning point. [L0613.034]
10. Attach quotes from real people and source links. [L0613.034]

#### Proxy buyer profile (for each buyer relationship)

1. Helplessness: what they cannot fix themselves and how watching the loved one suffer affects them (5 sourced examples). [L0613.035]
2. Guilt: what they blame themselves for and what they wish they had done (5 examples). [L0613.035]

Add at least 10 full proxy buyer narratives with links, the buyer's attention state, emotional entry point, sequence and purchase trigger. [L0613.035]

- A clearly named target viewer, such as a woman in a specific age range or life stage, makes the viewer feel the ad is for them. The speaker should be someone who fits that viewer, so the ad feels personal rather than broadcast. [L0707.009]

### Angle research and angle banks

- An angle is a separate layer from format and concept: it is the argument or approach the ad takes to the viewer. Do not confuse angle, concept and format when reading a competitor's data. [L0374.010]
- Mark any angle that is well-supported by avatar data but already saturated in the market. These angles have emotional validity but need a fresh mechanism or differentiated positioning to stand out against existing competitor ads. Saturation does not eliminate an angle; it signals the need for innovation within that emotional framework. [L0039.037]
- When a niche's main angle becomes saturated, reframe the same product for a different buyer, such as a gift bought for a partner instead of a purchase for oneself. Test that new angle as its own ad set before dropping the product. [L1315.051]
- Compare the buyer breakdown in the ad account (for example by gender) with the people shown in the creative. If the actual buyers differ from the people in the ad, make a new set of creatives aimed at the real buyer group. [L1315.052]
- Build a unique marketing angle by attacking the problem from different perspectives, so the same product can be marketed to different audiences or platforms. For example, Facebook for one group and TikTok for a younger group affected by the same problem. [L0513.016]
- Create ad angles that match the problem: one shows the product as protection from the cold, another shows use with coffee and friends, and a third shows the product as a gift. Men also buy it, so the audience can stay open to both genders. [L0492.045]
- Marketing angles generated for zodiac jewelry included showing off a star sign, a birthday or holiday gift, self-expression, and compatibility and connection between signs. A lead-generation quiz could return each buyer's matches as a one-page PDF and unlock a discount after completion. [L0549.035]
- Also target a secondary problem identified in the product map, such as convenience of using the product at home or saving time, within the same picture. (older) [L0580.013]
- Turn the research into concepts: from the collected data, list five ad angles (for example comfort, sustainability, more confidence, better sleep). Combine research with consumer-behavior principles such as survival, enjoyment of life, life extension, enjoyment of food and drink, envy, jealousy, curiosity, expression of beauty and style, economy, profit, convenience and efficiency to refine each angle. [L0902.013]
- Pick the most promising angles by checking what customers repeat in Amazon and Reddit reviews. [L0646.063]

#### Angle selection procedure

1. List the marketing angles for the product. [L0646.063]
2. Check what customers repeat in Amazon and Reddit reviews to see which angle is most likely to land. [L0646.063]
3. Ask ChatGPT which audience is more likely to respond, keeping in mind its data may only go back to 2021, and judge its answer against the review evidence. [L0646.063]
4. Produce one concept per angle, or at least the most promising one if time is short. [L0646.063]

[L0646.063]

- A video that mentions a product's flaw as a joke or confession can attract many comments and views, but views alone do not show buying intent. Test whether the audience actually buys before scaling a honesty-style angle, because it can work well or fail badly depending on the product. [L0655.001]
- A video with 100,000 views that converts well can be worth more than a video with one million views that attracts an unrelated audience, because conversion depends on the viewers' fit with the product. [L0795.028]

### Angle sheet and angle build

#### Angle sheet layout

One column per angle, rows are the ad structure. The values shown are for a pet hair removal brush and are placeholders for any product. Empty cells are marked with a dash.

| Row | Angle 1: dirty house / embarrassment | Angle 2: bathing the pet | Angle 3 | Angle 4 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Overview | Product; problem theme; target audience (lone pet owners) |, |, |, |
| Problem / hook | Pet hair gets everywhere; allergies flare up | Cannot wash the pet properly |, |, |
| Agitate (up to 3 rows) | Cannot breathe, house is dirty; everything feels like a mess; people do not like visiting | Water jet is weak; pet moves constantly, so no time to add more soap |, |, |
| Feeling (up to 2 rows) | Embarrassed, anxious; ill and low energy | Frustrated; wishes the pet could be bathed properly |, |, |
| Solution | Inexpensive, most effective pet hair cleaning tool | Spray nozzle with several adjustable settings, combined with the customer's favourite cleaning solution |, |, |
| What it does (feature list) | Sweeps and mops up hair; hair sticks to the brush fabric; removes a lot of hair in a few swipes with minimal effort; handles stubborn short and static hair; works on long and short hair; hair sticks like glue and is removed when the brush fills up |, |, |, |
| Meaning (2 to 4 rows) | House stays clean and hair-free; clothes stay cleaner and fresher longer; cleaning becomes quick, even enjoyable; the customer can relax |, |, |, |
| Outcome | Sleep easy; not embarrassed to have guests; able to breathe again |, |, |, |
| Avoid negative outcome (what if you do not buy) | Allergies; bacteria breeding ground; a filthy home |, |, |, |
| Social proof | Customer testimonials |, |, |, |
| Call to action | Discount on the product (e.g. 40%); second version: free gift with purchase today |, |, |, |

[L0392.001]

#### Building one angle

1. Choose the problem type and write one overview line naming the product, the problem theme and the target customer. [L0392.002]
2. Write the problem or hook: the visible symptom the customer sees first. [L0392.002]
3. Write two to three agitate lines that make the problem practical and concrete (what it does to breathing, cleanliness, time or social life). [L0392.002]
4. Write one or two feeling lines describing how the customer feels because of the problem. [L0392.002]
5. Write the solution in one line, naming the product category and its main claim. [L0392.002]
6. List the features in the "what it does" row, each as a short claim with a visible result. [L0392.002]
7. For each key feature, write a meaning line describing what this changes in the customer's home or day. [L0392.002]
8. Write the outcome: the emotional result the customer reaches after using the product. [L0392.002]
9. Write the avoid-negative-outcome row: what happens if the customer does not buy. [L0392.002]
10. Add social proof, such as customer testimonials that match this angle's problem. [L0392.002]
11. Write the call to action with a concrete offer. [L0392.002]
12. Start a new column for each different problem type, and keep columns separate so each one can be tested as its own angle. [L0392.002]

[L0392.002]

### Angle patterns for specific audiences

- Gift-based angle: frame the product as a gift from a partner or friend and describe the feeling it creates, so the customer sees a reason to buy for someone else or for themselves. Example for a ring, in italics: *My partner surprised me with this ring and it makes me feel seen every time I wear it.* Example for a keychain, in italics: *My sister gave me this so I always feel safe walking home at night.* [L0999.043]
- Cultural or identity-based angle: name a specific group or identity the product speaks to, and show how the product fits their life, which makes the creative more intimate and easier to target. Example: a jewelry piece for couples in a specific culture, described as worn for a special family occasion. Example: a hair brush for owners of large dogs that shed onto beds, shown with a before and after result. [L0999.044]
- Pattern for a niche angle: take a product that a broad audience sees as generic, name a specific situation in which it is used, and let the copy describe that situation. This works because the viewer can imagine using the product right away, which sells more than a general claim.
  - Example 1: a stainless steel travel mug for early-morning commutes on cold days. [L1161.037]
  - Example 2: a desk lamp for late-night study sessions in a shared room. [L1161.037]
- For products that appeal mainly to men, combine the product with a concrete situation where it is used. This narrows the message and helps a weak conversion rate. [L1161.038]
- A broad ad for a watch case asks whether you want to keep your watches in a box, which speaks to everyone and stands out less. A segment-specific ad speaks to the traveler's situation of choosing the right watch for each outfit on a trip abroad. [L0998.029]
- Models in an ad should look like the person the viewer wants to become, because viewers are more attracted to the product when the person in the ad matches their aspiration. [L1184.044]
- For ads targeting older audiences, use a younger person speaking to the older audience, because older viewers want to look young and do not identify with ads showing people their own age. [L1184.045]

### Angle patterns for products

- Show the target audience using the product in the real setting, such as a cyclist or snowboarder, and name the specific problem it solves. Avoid generic product shots on plain backgrounds for cold traffic. [L1225.046]
- Use a gifting angle with a product that is a gift, such as showing the item as the thing a buyer's family member would want. Keep the copy simple and clear about what the product is. [L1225.084]
- The same product can be marketed with different angles, such as a gift for couples, a memorial keepsake or a pregnancy milestone. Using different angles keeps the product fresh and gives you unique content. [L1171.041]
- Same product, different angle: take a product that already sells broadly and promote it to a specific audience with its own interest or problem, then brand the product page to match.
  - Example: a foldable mat promoted to yoga teachers for studio use. [L1185.028]
  - Example: a phone stand promoted to home bakers for recipe videos. [L1185.028]
- Angle for children's toys: position the toy as a way to reduce a child's screen time by offering a hands-on or educational activity instead.
  - Example of your own: a building kit that replaces tablet time with a 20-minute task. [L1176.037]
  - Example of your own: a drawing set pitched as a screen-free weekend activity for kids. [L1176.037]
- Family-benefit angle for educational toys: frame the product around reducing children's screen time and creating shared quality time with parents or grandparents.
  - Example: a wooden building kit that replaces an hour of tablet time. [L1185.030]
  - Example: a puzzle set designed for weekend time with grandchildren. [L1185.030]
- When a product has a technology feature, sell it as a classic or traditional look that keeps the buyer from falling behind on modern function. The formula is to name the timeless style the buyer already wants, then add the modern capability they fear missing. It works because it narrows the message to one specific audience and ties the product to status and belonging.
  - Example 1, in italics: *Keep the warm look of a wooden desk lamp without working under dim, outdated light.* [L0997.030]
  - Example 2, in italics: *Carry a classic leather wallet that still works with every new payment app.* [L0997.030]

### Naming angles and concepts

- An angle is the argument or approach the ad takes to the viewer. It is separate from the concept and the format. [L0374.010]
- Naming: for each distinct angle, give a clear name. [L0039.009]

#### Angle-naming prompt

```
Combine the fears and angles discovered in customer research with the gaps between what competitors currently advertise and what the market isn't hearing. For each distinct angle, provide a clear name, state the underlying fear and mechanism in one line, cite the supporting evidence from customer data and market gaps, assess whether competitors are already saturating this angle or whether it remains open territory, and rank by expected strength, with well-supported customer fears that competitors ignore rising to the top.
```

[L0039.009]

- To give a name to what people feel but have not yet expressed, use verbal creativity. This is part of introducing a new product to a market that does not yet know it. [L0330.031]
- Renaming an old product can create a new market appeal. The South Beach Diet was initially named "Modified Carbohydrate Diet" and failed until it was renamed. Apple's iPod was marketed as "1,000 songs in your pocket" though it was not the first MP3 player. [L1356.055]

#### Angle-choice prompt

```
From the angles you listed, choose the most unique one, meaning one that most competitors in this niche do not use. Explain why it is unique, how often buyers mention the underlying feeling, and which emotion and desired outcome it connects. Keep the answer as a short paragraph.
```

[L1140.019]

#### Planning a new ad (concept development)

1. State the problem in plain words, for example that you want to sell this product. [L1366.086]
2. Restate the problem in a different way, for example that you want to introduce the unique aspects of the product to the prospect. [L1366.086]
3. Restate it again in terms of the buyer's experience, for example that the product should be easy to buy and seem fun. [L1366.086]
4. Choose the restatement that feels closest to the ad you want to write. [L1366.086]
5. List several big ideas for that restatement and pick the one or two that make the most sense. [L1366.086]
6. Visualize how the concept fits into the ad and check it against the restatement. [L1366.086]
7. Stop and incubate. [L1366.086]
8. Write the headline, then the subheadline, then the first sentence. [L1366.086]
9. Block-diagram the finished ad to check its flow. [L1366.086]

[L1366.086]

### Unique selling points and value propositions

- Value propositions can be functional (solve a technical or practical need, typical for tech or electronics) or emotional (typical for kids' products and beauty products). Define one value proposition per customer archetype based on which reason drives the purchase. [L0902.010]
- List the unique selling points of best-selling products, such as manufacturing process, eco-friendly features, press coverage or charity donations, because these can serve as credible marketing angles. [L0902.012]
- Compare products by a single value-based claim that rivals cannot easily copy, because copied general claims become commonplace and lose value. Look for a unique, specific, verifiable advantage. [L1261.082]
- The USP formula from Rosser Reeves has three parts: the product must actually do what the copy says it does, the benefit must be original compared with competitors, and the promise must target a core desire the prospect already has. Desire cannot be created, only awakened. [L0756.030]
- The unique selling proposition in the offer must make the service different, typically through the phrasing "The only service that...". A USP can be created in three ways:
  1. By genuinely unique features like a proprietary system or patented technology. [L1356.053]
  2. By labeling a common feature as unique because competitors do not talk about it. [L1356.053]
  3. By giving an old thing a new name. [L1356.053]
- Labeling a common feature as unique works by highlighting something every competitor also has but no one mentions. For example, a manufacturer's gold-plated connectors that all rivals also use but never advertised. The reader treats the newly highlighted detail as distinctive. [L1356.054]

### Models, presenters and identity in creatives

- Ads should use a wide variety of avatars, including different genders, ages and ethnicities, to promote the same product. This variety allows testing which audience responds best. [L1187.021]
- Models in an ad should look like the person the viewer wants to become. [L1184.044]
- A well-known person can be used as an opponent or challenge rather than an endorser, because a challenge creates a story and an endorsement only adds a name. Build the ad around the contest and make the product the thing being challenged. Get written permission before publishing any name, since an unauthorized use caused a legal dispute in the original case. [L1366.084]

### Copy flow across stages on multi-page stores (older)

Units in this group come from the 2021-22 course and are marked older.

- Long-form sales pages make it easier to test different messages and to address different awareness segments. Traffic sources can also be used to send each awareness segment to a different message. (older) [L0904.011]
- When a store has many product pages, write the copy so it starts at the Problem Aware stage instead of writing separate copy for each stage. Copy that starts at Problem Aware works for visitors at that stage and at every stage above it up to purchase. (older) [L0904.012]
- Copy that starts at a later stage such as Product Aware does not work for visitors who are at an earlier stage. Copy that starts at Unaware works for all stages, but it is harder to write well. (older) [L0904.013]
- People who are at Problem Aware or above are easy to target because they already know their pain and what they want to solve. Using one copy flow that starts with the pain is simpler than writing different copy for each awareness stage. (older) [L0904.015]

#### Copy flow procedure (older)

1. Name the customer's pain or problem first, since Problem Aware visitors recognize it. [L0904.014]
2. Build the desire for a solution by showing how the solution addresses that problem. [L0904.014]
3. Lead the reader through the options to the point of purchase within the same copy. [L0904.014]

[L0904.014]

- Example for a surfboard store selling to beginners (older): the Problem Aware stage is the realization that they have no board and cannot surf without one. The Solution Aware stage is choosing between renting and buying. The Product Aware stage is comparing beginner boards by budget, shape, style and brand. The Ninja Aware stage is choosing a specific brand, shape and style from a specific seller. This course adds Ninja Aware after Product Aware, which is not part of Schwartz's five stages. [L0904.016]
- At the Ninja Aware stage, the solution itself creates the desire. Once a buyer understands how a solution works, they want the products that deliver it, so copy for late-stage buyers should connect the product to the solution the buyer has already accepted. (older) [L0904.020]

### Testing, planning and checklists

- Ads aimed at product-aware audiences differ from ads aimed at unaware audiences, a framework covered in the classic book Breakthrough Advertising. Creating creatives for unaware audiences is a way to grow a product that has already reached its aware market. [L1127.029]
- Ads that run a long time can keep working even after a product is obsolete, as long as the core need and buyer motivation are unchanged. Work out the buyer's underlying need so the copy stays valid across product cycles. [L1366.070]

#### Pre-launch ad checklist

1. Does it tap into a desire the audience already has? [L1348.026]
2. Does it show the desirable outcome the customer can reach with the product? [L1348.026]
3. Does it future-pace the viewer, letting them picture life after using the product? [L1348.026]
4. Does it show social proof, such as evidence that other people already use it? [L1348.026]
5. Is there an authority signal, such as an expert endorsement, where the product category makes one credible (for example an orthopedic surgeon backing a back-support product)? [L1348.026]
6. Does the angle match the buyer's journey stage? [L1348.026]

[L1348.026]

### Avatar documents

Write the avatar before any copy. Use the ten questions below to build it, then check the result against an example persona. [L1370.001, L1370.002]

**Ten questions about the target buyer, answered in this order:**

1. What keeps them awake at night, or what worries them? [L1370.001]
2. What are they afraid of? [L1370.001]
3. What makes them angry, and who do they blame? [L1370.001]
4. What are their top three daily frustrations? [L1370.001]
5. Which trends are changing their business or life now and later? [L1370.001]
6. What do they secretly want most? [L1370.001]
7. Does the way they make decisions have a built-in bias? [L1370.001]
8. Do they use their own vocabulary? [L1370.001]
9. Who else sells something similar to them, and how? [L1370.001]
10. Who has tried to sell them something similar, and why did it fail? [L1370.001]

**Example persona: liquid instant coffee for busy adults** [L1427.072]

| Element | Detail |
|---|---|
| Age | 20 to 35 |
| Gender | Mostly women |
| Income | Mid to high |
| Education | University educated |
| Main wants | Focus on what matters; skip mundane tasks |
| Fears | Falling behind; feeling overwhelmed |
| Desire | Great-tasting coffee, instantly, that helps them feel alert in the morning [L1427.072] |

### Research before writing

- Research the buyer before writing any copy, because the copy only works if the writer truly understands the buyer. [L1370.002]
- Visualise a typical recipient's whole day, from arrival at work to how and when their mail reaches them. Note what else occupies their attention at that moment. [L1370.002]
- Study the reader before the product. Find the features that match the reader's needs and build the letter around them. A letter that starts from the buyer's reactions and presents only the matching product features is almost always effective. [L1369.039]
- Let the buyer's priorities drive the copy, not the seller's. A sales letter gets no live feedback to correct a misunderstanding. [L1370.004]
- A corporate buyer weighing a donation or purchase typically asks three things: [L1370.004]
  1. What benefit justifies the cost?
  2. Who else already chose this?
  3. Where will the money come from in the budget? [L1370.004]

### Ad angles and concept building

- Define the ad angle before the script. An ad angle is a specific take on a problem for a target audience. [L1425.027]
- Not every product solves a problem. Some products fulfil a need, such as self-expression, identity, or a hobby. For these, connect the ad emotionally to the desired feeling rather than to a problem. [L1426.019]

**Lateral thinking exercise for a stuck ad concept:**

1. Pick a random source of words, such as a shuffled set of words or a dictionary. [L1366.087]
2. Pull out the first three words you see. [L1366.087]
3. Force a connection between those three words and the product you are selling. [L1366.087]
4. Build an ad concept from the connection, keeping the selling goal in mind. [L1366.087]

### Awareness stage and funnel messaging

- For audiences who do not yet know a product category exists, or do not realise they have a problem it solves, do not push a purchase. Open with the symptom or desire they already feel, such as tiredness. Explain the benefits and present the product as a possible answer, so the first step is awareness, not a sale. [L1386.018]
- Showing a buy-now offer to people who are not ready to buy wastes ad spend. It also drives away prospects who would have converted later. Serve the right message at each funnel stage to keep those prospects in the funnel instead of losing them. [L1386.019]

### On-screen models

- Use one consistent on-screen model across all videos. In competitor videos, a consistent model increased sales, especially when the product targeted women. Using her in every video can build recognition. [L1444.032]

## Competitor and ad-library research

### Research tools at a glance

| Tool | What it shows | Cost | Use it for | Source ids |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Meta Ad Library | Ads running on Meta platforms, active and past | Free | Finding long-running ads and reading competitor creative | L0039.019, L0039.013, L0637.011 |
| Kalodata | Top-performing ad scripts, videos and revenue by product | Paid | Choosing proven ads by sales data | L0039.018, L0901.024, L1187.024 |
| AdvertSuite | Live ads on Facebook, Instagram, Google and YouTube, searchable by keyword and attributes | Paid | Seeing what works now, not only historical examples | L0196.055 |
| TikTok Creative Center | Trending hooks and advertisers in a niche | Free | Finding paid-traffic winners on TikTok | L1374.006 |
| Minea | Competitor store ads and run length | Paid | Spotting scaled ads and repeated hooks | L0871.069 |
| Foreplay | Ad board and swipe file, no metrics | About 50 USD per month | Collecting inspiration into boards | L0692.050, L1348.010 |
| Afterlip | Trending products and features | 9 USD per month plan, down from 99 USD per month | Product discovery; check saturation first | L0349.013 |
| Trello | Customizable research database | Free version sufficient | Storing captured ads | L0196.056 |
| FireShot | Full-page screenshots in Chrome | Chrome extension | Capturing long landing pages | L0196.057 |

- Do not judge the free Meta Ad Library by search results alone; check run length and duplicates for each ad before treating it as a winner. [L0374.031, L0523.042]

### Finding winners: run time, spend and scale signals

#### Run time as a shortcut

- Ads that have run for a long time are usually profitable, so run duration is a useful shortcut for spotting winners. Model the headline, image, video and copy of ads that have been running for months. [L0523.042]
- Any ad running for months has been validated as a successful winner in the free Meta Ad Library and can be swiped for analysis. [L0039.019, L0039.013]
- In the Meta Ads Library, the ads that have run longest are usually the ones with the best return on ad spend. Scroll to the bottom of the results to find them. Use them for inspiration on structure and copy, but do not copy them. [L0667.010]
- Caution: do not assume the longest-running ad is the winner. Some advertisers keep ads running without sales to mislead competitors. Check running days together with duplicates and traffic before copying an ad. [L0374.031]
- Running time and duplicates together give a stronger signal than either alone. Where an ad appears as many separate variations, treat it as proven. [L0707.001]
- Look for a creative that runs in many ads at once; the lesson uses 8 or more ads as the scaling signal. [L0398.021]
- Recent-launch check: the Brands tracker counts new ads per week, and 3 to 5 new ads per week signals active scaling. [L0374.032]

#### Spend and brand size

- Prioritize big brands that spend heavily on Facebook, for example around 1 to 5 million USD per month, because they test creative constantly. [L0398.021]
- Study what large brands run and copy their layout, fonts, colors and ad formats. They have spent heavily on testing, so their proven choices are a useful starting point. [L0692.016, L0646.041]
- Check the Facebook Ad Library for the ads large brands in your niche keep running, because those brands test heavily and keep what works. Use the winning styles as a starting point, then test them for your own product and niche. [L0646.041]
- Research direct competitors that sell the same product and, above all, large brands in the niche, because large brands spend heavily on testing creative ideas and marketing angles. Save their ads and landing pages in one sheet for reference. [L0902.011]

#### Recency and engagement

- Find competitor creatives from the last two weeks by searching 5 to 10 product keywords and related hashtags on TikTok. Recent videos are less likely to have been shown to your audience. [L1377.027]
- A good creative to test is one uploaded recently, not yet used by many competitors, and already getting a good like rate on PP Ads. A recent competitor video with a strong like rate shows real engagement. [L1382.022]
- On TikTok, compare a creative's likes with its ad impressions. Strong impressions and a good like count mean the creative resonates and is worth replicating. [L0895.033]
- Kalodata's Video & Ad list shows each ad with revenue, view count and post date. Use these figures to pick hooks from ads that already sold, not ads picked at random. It has an Export button for the list. [L0901.024]

#### Stopped ads

- If a competitor stopped a creative for a product, the cause may be account issues rather than poor performance. You can still test the product, but check results after a few days and change the creative, offer or market if sales do not come. [L1219.048]

### Searching the Meta Ad Library step by step

#### Competitor research in the Ad Library

1. Open the competitor's Facebook page. [L0649.063]
2. In the right column, click Page transparency. [L0649.063]
3. Click See more to view the page creation date, name changes and the number of people managing the page. [L0649.063]
4. Click the Ad Library link, or the button to see all ads, to view active and past ads. [L0649.063]
5. Check the start date, format and copy of each ad, and switch the country to see regional ads. [L0649.063]
6. Revisit the page regularly to see which ads they keep running. [L0649.063]

#### Finding and replicating winning creatives

1. Open the Meta Ad Library and search your niche and the competitors and large brands in it. [L0398.021]
2. Prioritize big brands that spend heavily on Facebook (see spend guidance above). [L0398.021]
3. Look for creatives that run in many ads at once; 8 or more ads is the scaling signal used in the lesson. [L0398.021]
4. Compare the creatives of the same brand and note the hook that repeats in the first seconds while the later clips change. [L0398.021]
5. Replicate the repeated hook in your own ads and test it against your own video. [L0398.021]

#### Using the Ad Library for wording and downloads

- Search the Facebook Ad Library for the niche, such as home decor, to find wording ideas for primary text and headlines. [L0642.051]
- Search the product name in the Meta Ad Library with All ads selected, Active status filter on and country set to United States. [L0707.001]
- Check whether the same video runs many times as separate ad variations, since many active variations signal a proven ad. [L0707.001]
- To download a video from the Ad Library: play the ad, right-click it, choose Save video as, and type the file name with the extension.mp4. If the file is saved with another extension, download it and rename the extension to.mp4 so it opens as a video. [L0638.045]
- Meta Ad Library lets you download a competitor's ad creative for review. Save the files and study the hook, pacing and format before building your own test version. Do not copy the footage itself. [L0335.063]
- Download the video creatives of shortlisted products from the Meta Ads Library and save them in the shared research folder. Use them as a reference when briefing your own test ads, so the team works from the same examples. [L1173.046]

#### AdvertSuite ad research (5 steps)

1. Define a S.M.A.R.T. objective for what ad types you want to find and why. [L0196.003]
2. Select the 'Keywords' search mode and choose 'Ad Text', 'Comments', or 'Landing Page Text' as the search field. Filter by country, date range, ad position, demographics and technology if needed. Sort by 'Longest Running' or by engagement (likes, comments, shares). [L0196.003, L0196.055]
3. Start with broad keywords related to your industry, then add filters. Examine the results to see what is working now. [L0196.003]
4. Capture each ad in a Trello board: [L0196.003, L0196.056]
   - screenshot the full ad from source;
   - copy the text to a Google Doc and link it;
   - add a link to the landing page;
   - screenshot the landing page (use FireShot Chrome extension for long pages) [L0196.057];
   - screenshot the AdvertSuite details page;
   - capture relevant comments.
5. Analyze each ad by asking 30 questions, including: who the advertiser targets, what the short-term goal is, which features and benefits are shared, what the core attention grabber is, what mood is conveyed, which objections are addressed, and which calls to action are used. [L0196.003]

#### Trello as the research database

- Create columns (lists) by keyword or category. Add cards with ad details, labels (platform, ad type), description (AdvertSuite search settings) and comments. [L0196.056]
- AdvertSuite lets you filter by country, date range, ad position (newsfeed vs. sidebar), gender, language, age and technology used. [L0196.055]
- FireShot is a Chrome extension that takes full-page screenshots of pages longer than the screen, used to capture complete landing pages for analysis. [L0196.057]

### Tracking competitors in the brand tracker

#### What the tracker shows

- A tracked brand's detail page has these tabs: Overview, Ad Copies, Ad Headlines, Ad Hooks, Landing Pages, Personas, Concepts, Angles, Desires, Emotions, Awareness Stages and USPs. Each tab breaks down that element across the brand's ads, so you can check which hooks, angles or desires a competitor uses most. [L0772.044, L0892.014]
- Together these tabs show how a competitor is positioning and selling right now, based on its live ads. [L0892.014]
- A competitor's top personas, concepts, angles, USPs, emotions and desires come from its live ads, so they show what it is actually running. Copying or varying the strongest of these is faster than guessing the strategy. [L0892.015]
- The tracker's concept categories are Demo / How-It Works, Before-And-After, Educational Explainer, Social Proof / Reviews, Promotion / Discount, Problem-Agitate-Solve, Bundle / Multi-Pack Offer and Social Proof Emphasis. Check which of these a competitor scales most. [L0374.011]
- The tracker's angle categories in the example included Problem-Agitate-Solve, Customer Before-And-After Reveal, At-Home Microneedling Substitute, Budget Comparison, Comparison Vs Microneedling, Side-By-Side Comparison and After Demonstration. Each angle is tracked with the number of ads that use it. [L0374.012]
- In the awareness-stage view, the sort control offers Usage over 7 days or 30 days and Longest Running. Hooks and landing pages that appear across many ads or stay live for months are the strongest candidates to study first. [L0892.037]

#### Procedure: analyse a competitor brand

1. Open the brand and read the overview cards: top landing pages, personas, concepts, angles, desires, emotions, awareness stages and USPs. [L0374.032]
2. Count the new ads uploaded each week; 3 to 5 new ads per week signals active scaling. [L0374.032]
3. Check ad attribution by format; if almost all ads are video, the brand is scaling video. [L0374.032]
4. Open the Ad Copies tab and identify the copy with the most attributed ads; that is the main winning copy. Then check the headlines and hooks. [L0374.032]
5. Open the Landing Pages tab, note the number of pages and the share of ads sent to each. [L0374.032]
6. Open Personas and Concepts to see which audiences and formats the brand uses. [L0374.032]
7. Open Angles, Desires, Emotions, Awareness Stages and USPs. [L0374.032]
8. Open the top ads, read the ad details (running days, duplicates, landing page, price) and generate the transcript. [L0374.032]
9. Download the top video for frame-by-frame analysis. [L0374.032]

#### Reading a top ad's transcript

- In a tracked brand's overview, opening a video ad from the list gives you its transcript. Read the spoken hook and script word for word before rebuilding a similar ad. [L0772.045]
- Video ads in a brand's list can be opened for transcripts, speakable scripts, and framework or pattern analysis. Use these to see how a competitor's ad is structured before writing your own. [L0892.017]

#### Export hooks and generate variations

1. Open the brand and go to the Ad Hooks tab. [L0892.016]
2. Click Export to download the hooks as a CSV file. [L0892.016]
3. Import the CSV into an AI tool. [L0892.016]
4. Ask the AI for more hooks similar to the exported ones. [L0892.016]
- Pro tip: exporting top hooks, personas and angles from a brand and feeding them into an AI tool such as Claude can surface further personas and angles beyond those the tool lists. [L0892.018]

#### Worked case: acne-scar serum brand

- Case: an acne-scar serum brand was on the tracker with 133 active ads, tracked since 6 May 2026, and had been added 22 hours before the data was pulled, so counts were still filling in. [L0374.041]
- It uploaded 3 to 5 new ads per week, attributed almost only to video, with no image or carousel ads. [L0374.041]
- 133 ads ran the same main ad copy, whose headline reached 23,000+ people. [L0374.041]
- The top persona was people with acne scars, followed by budget-conscious skincare shoppers and adults with acne scars. [L0374.041]
- The top desire was fading acne scars, the top emotions were hope and relief, and the top USPs were a 90-day money-back guarantee, a microcrystal technology as the main mechanism, and bundle pricing under $40. [L0374.041]
- Traffic went almost only to product pages: 125 ads (81.2%) to the main product page and 8 ads (5.2%) to a second page, with no listicles, advertorials or pre-sell pages. [L0374.041]
- The analysis showed the brand lagging on its funnel, so a similar product with a stronger funnel and a better offer could compete. [L0374.041]
- The top video was downloaded, transcribed, analysed frame by frame in Gemini, and its script adapted to a new product. [L0374.041]

#### Worked example: supplement brand

- A supplement brand with 67 active ads had Promotion / Discount as its top concept, Fast and Free Shipping as its top USP, and a limited-time deal as its top desire. [L0892.039]
- This combination shows a brand that relies on urgency and price incentives. It can be copied directly or varied with a different angle. [L0892.039]

### Reverse-engineering a winning video in Kalodata

#### Procedure

1. In Kalodata, open the product page and set the region to United States and the date range to Last 30 Days. [L0707.001]
2. Check that the product sells at scale in Core Metrics: Main Revenue, Item Sold and Avg. Unit Price. [L0707.001]
3. Open the Video & Ad tab and pick the video ad with the highest views and revenue in the period. [L0707.001]
4. Watch the video and note the hook, the problem named, the testimonial structure, the solution, the benefits, the social proof and the call to action. [L0707.001]
5. Search the product name in the Meta Ad Library (see Ad Library settings above). [L0707.001]
6. Check whether the same video runs many times as separate ad variations. [L0707.001]
7. Use the findings to build your own version of the structure, not a copy of the video. [L0707.001]

#### Reference numbers

- Winning reference ad: about 8 million views and about 165k revenue in the last 30 days, with the video running about 1 minute 57 seconds on the player. [L0707.006]
- Kalodata's Video & Ad view lists competitor video ads for a product, and the Storyboard Export lets you export an ad's storyboard for analysis. Highest Revenue Videos and their conversion rates show which ad creatives generate the most sales. [L1187.024]
- Good ad editing and detailed bottom-funnel creatives indicate a product's ads are worth studying and possibly copying in a customized form. Look for creatives that show the product in use or in a result-focused way. [L1187.023]

#### Worked case: calcium multi-balm stick

- Case: a Korean calcium multi-balm stick, sold in the United States and on TikTok Shop, reached about 50k revenue per day and about 1.5 million in the last 30 days. [L0707.020]
- Its best ad, a phone-filmed creator testimonial, reached about 8 million views and about 165k revenue in the same period. [L0707.020]
- The ad ran about 1 minute 57 seconds and opened with a woman naming the product as a Botox-like balm to stop the scroll. [L0707.020]
- She then showed a before and after image, named smoker lines and under-eye darkness, told a story about an aunt who smoked for over 20 years, and added her own insecurity. [L0707.020]
- She then claimed she is a nurse, listed adenosine, glutathione and a patented calcium-vitamin D ingredient with about ten benefits in a row, cited five-star reviews and a four-week wait from stock shortage, and ended with urgency to act fast. [L0707.020]
- The same video ran as a repeated Meta ad, with about 6,500 keyword results in the Ad Library. [L0707.020]

### Selecting and editing test videos from Kalodata

#### Procedure

1. Open the Video & Ad list in Kalodata and set the time filter to Last 30 Days. [L0704.001]
2. Look for videos with high view counts and strong sales, which signal a viral, trending ad. [L0704.001]
3. Choose 12 to 24 videos for a test, starting with at least 12. [L0704.001]
4. Take half of the selected videos (about six) from page 1 and the rest from pages 2 and 3. [L0704.001, L0704.012]
5. Keep only videos that show a real person; drop abstract or product-only videos. [L0704.001]
6. Drop videos whose hook or demonstrated outcome does not match what your product delivers, even if the hook itself is strong. [L0704.001]
7. Drop videos whose spoken language is not English, since you cannot check or match their message to your store. [L0704.001, L0704.011]
8. Do not spend much time judging production quality; the sales data is the main signal. [L0704.001, L0704.005]
9. In CapCut, cut every part that mentions TikTok Shop or Orange Cart. [L0704.001]
10. Cut every offer that is not on your landing page, including buy one get one free if your website does not show it. [L0704.001]
11. Make no other changes: add no new hooks and no extra edits to videos that already sell. [L0704.001]

#### Why this selection works

- Do not judge a video mainly by how polished it looks. If a video shows strong sales, it is already working, so its quality matters less than its results. [L0704.005]
- Pulling some winners from deeper result pages targets ads that fewer competitors are looking at, which gives the test fresher material than only the top results. [L0704.013]
- Spending a long time deciding whether a video is good wastes time. Use the view and sales data first and sort the videos on that basis. [L0704.015]
- Kalodata's result list offers a Download Video (Without Watermark) option, which gives a clean file to edit before running the ad. [L0704.017]

### Analysing the psychology of winning ads

#### Prompt: psychological pattern analysis of a swipe file

Use this prompt unchanged when you have a collection of successful ads:

```text
When you receive a collection of successful ads, study each one to uncover the psychological pattern underneath the wording. For every ad, identify which emotion it activates (fear or desire), the core logic that makes its promise credible, the specific opening technique that halts scrolling, and the sequence of beats it follows. Then group the ads by shared emotional target and persuasion approach, identify fears the avatar likely holds that none of these ads address, and classify where the audience sits on Schwartz's five-stage awareness model (Unaware through Most Aware).
```

[L0039.003]

#### Swipe file size

- Gather 5 to 10 winning ad scripts to analyze as your swipe file. If using Kalodata, take the top performers. If using the free Meta Ad Library, any ad running for months is validated as a proven winner. [L0039.013]

#### Ad style analysis

- Always study what competitors are doing in their ad copy and improve on what is already working. Use competitive copywriting as inspiration for your own differentiation, not as a template to replicate. [L0206.005]
- Ad style analysis compares each pair of styles with at least 10 examples each for the first pair, and tracks pattern changes over time. Pairs: [L0613.016]
  - professional vs user-generated content;
  - emotional vs logical appeals;
  - benefit-focused (bright side) vs problem-focused (dark side);
  - simple vs complex explanation;
  - short-form vs long-form;
  - serious vs humorous tone;
  - male vs female presenters;
  - solo presenter vs group;
  - studio vs real-world setting;
  - text-heavy vs image-focused;
  - technical vs lifestyle framing;
  - identity-led vs benefit-led.
- Also note outliers that succeed despite going against the trend. [L0613.016]
- Model proven landing pages and ads instead of inventing new ones and hoping they work. Find what competitors already run, such as opt-in pages, sales pages or quiz pages, and build something similar before testing refinements. Following a proven model saves a lot of time and money. [L0523.043]
- Copying one source closely is imitation that reads as a knockoff, while borrowing from many sources is research that produces something new. Copy the reasoning behind a style, such as why an ad hook works for its audience, not just its surface look. [L1343.003]
- Copying a competitor's ad without understanding why it works, and without setting expectations, is a common cause of failure. Competitor research is useful only to extract transferable lessons, not to clone their ads. [L1348.002]

### Analysing hooks, visuals and comments

#### Hooks and visuals

1. Analyze 20 to 25 of the most successful hooks from TikTok, Instagram and Facebook ads, identify the patterns that work most often, and note which hooks have run longest. [L0613.011]
2. Analyze visuals: picture of the benefit, picture of the problem, picture of the product, product in action, environments, people shown, what visuals create belief, production quality (professional vs authentic UGC), color schemes and text overlay styles. [L0613.011]
3. Analyze at least 100 comments on viral posts, grouped by questions, objections, enthusiasm and testimonials. Note sentiment, 'wish I had known' and 'I need this because' comments, tagging behavior, and identity-resonance comments. [L0613.011]
4. Study emotional storytelling: transformation versus feature-benefit ads, character arcs, before-state portrayal, vulnerability moments, and at least 10 ads that tap identity-level emotion. [L0613.011]
5. Map content structures (see table below) and note the balance of emotion versus logic, typical ad length, objection handling and narrative patterns. [L0613.011, L0613.013]

#### Content structures in winning content

| Structure | Description | Source ids |
|---|---|---|
| Symptom → Problem → Solution → Product → Offer | Full funnel from symptom | L0613.013 |
| Problem → Solution → Product → Offer | Starts at the problem | L0613.013 |
| Solution → Product → Offer | Starts at the solution | L0613.013 |
| Product → Offer | Starts at the product | L0613.013 |
| Offer only | Starts at the price or deal | L0613.013 |
| Identity → Problem → Solution → Product → Offer | Identity-first approach | L0613.013 |

- Deliverables for this section: 20 to 25 viral hooks with links; 20 to 30 representative comments; 15 to 20 visual approaches; 7 to 10 effective structure patterns; 10 to 15 successful calls to action; 5 to 7 trending visual styles; 3 to 5 trending hashtags. [L0613.013]

#### Problem and solution messaging

- Problem-and-solution messaging on the product page and in the ads is an effective way to explain why a product is worth buying. Check how a competitor presents the problem and solution before writing your own. [L1172.044]
- Competitor analysis on the landing page: [L0708.039]
  1. Open each competitor landing page you found.
  2. Note the marketing angles, the copywriting and the offers they use.
  3. Identify weaknesses such as brand colors or layout that you could improve.
  4. Use these findings to create a stronger version and beat the competition.

### Interrupt-style ad models

Collect interrupt-style ad models:

1. Search Google Images for tabloid newspaper headlines. [L0523.033]
2. Note the unusual or shocking images used to grab attention. [L0523.033]
3. Note how headlines stay short and make the reader curious. [L0523.033]
4. Adapt these patterns to your own product and audience in your ads. [L0523.033]

### Finding gaps and building differentiation

- Gaps in your analysis are fears or mechanisms that the avatar likely has but that none of the winning competitor ads address. These are white-space openings worth testing. [L0039.034]
- Identifying gaps means recognizing unaddressed emotional pain, unmet anxieties or unstated objections in the customer data that the swipe file does not hit. These signal potential differentiation angles. [L0039.034]
- Before analyzing your audience, do competitor creative research first. Understanding how competitors frame problems and structure messaging simplifies the audience investigation, because you already know which angles and language resonate in your market. [L0258.027]
- Competitor creative research process: [L0258.005]
  1. Identify your 3 most important competitors.
  2. For each competitor, find their 3 most commonly used creative types (UGC, lifestyle images, high-production video, memes, etc.).
  3. For each creative type, document: the concept or angle (testimonial, unboxing, advertorial, problem-solution), hooks used in the first 3 seconds, problems and desires addressed, benefits, features, pain points, objections overcome, target character attributes and age, scenery, and slang or buzzwords.
- Start every market analysis by checking how many similar products have already advertised to the same prospects. Competitors' ads are the best evidence; a few hours of research should gather samples of every competing ad. [L0330.048]
- For a new competitor that scales, the ad is usually the main reason it works, not the website. The product matters most, but the ad hook and visual approach are what sell it. [L0335.044]
- Afterlip shows trending products and features beyond Dropispy. Check that the products found are not oversaturated before testing them. [L0349.013]
- Review competitors' Facebook Ad Library and identify the ads they run for a long time, because repeated ads signal winners. Analyse their storyline and marketing angle, then replicate or adapt that angle for your own product. [L0902.016]

### TikTok research

#### Finding a winning hook on TikTok

1. Open the TikTok Creative Center. [L1374.006]
2. Select your niche. [L1374.006]
3. Look for products being sold with paid traffic in that niche. [L1374.006]
4. Identify the hook, structure, and creative style that repeat across the advertisers that appear to be working. [L1374.006]
5. Replicate the same structure and hook with your own product, adapting sound, visuals, and presentation. [L1374.006]

#### Value and aspiration

- Competitor analysis for TikTok means identifying what value competitors offer their audience through education, entertainment or aspiration, and then providing that same kind of value. Aspiration works through people wanting to be like a respected figure who uses the product. It is typically used in influencer-led categories such as beauty and cosmetics. [L1374.007]
- Study TikTok videos of similar products, log why they work, then reproduce the style rather than copying a single post. [L0561.041]

#### Researching before filming

1. Search for other sellers of the same product. [L1381.036]
2. Find videos for that product with decent views. [L1381.036]
3. Study how they made theirs, including their text and sound, and replicate the approach in your own videos. [L1381.036]
4. Save viral sounds to favorites for later use. [L1381.036]

### Idea boards and inspiration in the editing app

#### Edits app: brainstorming and ideas

- Edits includes a brainstorming section that suggests content styles which perform for other accounts in a similar niche. Use it to test formats before producing them. [L1453.005]
- The Ideas tab has three sections: [L1453.012]
  - Stickies (sticky notes);
  - Reels (saved reels, whose audio can be reused directly);
  - Collections (folders you create by category, e.g. by location, person, or topic).
- To add a sticky note: Ideas tab > plus button at the bottom > sticky note. Sticky notes can be given a different color and act as a quick place to note video ideas. [L1453.011]
- Process for organizing video ideas in Edits: [L1453.013]
  1. Save reels with audio you want to use in the Reels section of the Ideas tab.
  2. Add sticky notes for ideas that come up while watching other content.
  3. Group saved reels into Collections by category, such as location, collaborator, or video type.
  4. Use the saved audio and notes when producing each video.

#### Inspiration tab

- The Inspiration tab is a Reels-style feed of popular content, filterable by accounts you follow. It has no like, comment, follow or send function, so it is for browsing only. [L1453.014]
- Actions on a reel in the Inspiration tab: save it, use its audio immediately for editing, or add a sticky note. The 'use audio' action opens the audio directly in the editor. [L1453.015]

### Swipe files and boards

#### What a swipe file is

- A swipe file is a digital or analog archive of ads, creatives, headlines, page layouts and other material you have saved from others. Open it when you need ideas and reuse the patterns, not the exact content. Photos taken with a phone are enough to build one. [L1343.006]
- Keep a swipe file of brands that inspire you and review it regularly, for example every other day. This shows how similar products are marketed in your niche. [L1194.007]

#### Building a swipe file

1. When you see an ad, landing page or creative worth reusing, save it to your swipe file immediately. [L1343.007]
2. Keep the file in a form you actually use, digital or analog, and add to it regularly. [L1343.007]
3. When you need inspiration for a new ad or creative, open the file and look for patterns that match your product and audience. [L1343.007]
4. Adapt the pattern to your own offer rather than copying it directly. [L1343.007]

#### Boards in Foreplay and similar tools

- Foreplay is a swipe file tool where brands save ads. Use it to collect proven examples, such as Black Friday ads from e-commerce brands, before producing your own creatives. [L0692.050]
- Foreplay is a paid ad inspiration tool, about 50 USD per month. It saves ads from the Facebook Ad Library into boards through a Chrome extension. It works as a mood board of ideas rather than a performance tracker, because it does not show metrics. [L1348.010]
- Collect ad inspiration in this order: [L1348.011]
  1. Find ads in the Facebook Ad Library and check how many days each has been running, as longer-running ads suggest performance.
  2. Save ads that look like good performers or show good design practice into a board in an ad collection tool such as Foreplay, using its Chrome extension.
  3. Follow industry experts who post their ads and build a swipe file from them.
  4. Analyze saved ads for the psychological principle, layout and spacing that make them work.

#### Reverse-engineering a saved ad

1. Pick a product, ad or brand you admire. [L1343.035]
2. Write down what it leaves out or could have done better. [L1343.035]
3. Create your own version that fills one of those gaps. [L1343.035]
4. Compare your version with the original to see which choices are your own tendencies. [L1343.035]

### Automating competitive ad intelligence

- Set a trigger for when a competitor uploads a new ad to their ad library. The automation downloads the ad, optionally uses an AI step to transcribe it, feeds it to Claude to rewrite it for your brand's voice and offer, and saves the adapted version to Google Drive or Google Docs. This builds a continuously updated competitive creative reference library with zero manual effort. [L0287.018]

### Older advice (2018)

- Older advice (2018): competitor promo text, such as an offer of free shipping, and better product images can lift CTR. Test similar promo text or images if you can afford the offer. [L1274.067]

#### Further details

- The Meta Ads Library is a platform resource where you can view ads from competitors in your niche. Use it to study successful creative patterns (hooks, messaging, calls-to-action), then create your own ads inspired by these insights but always with at least one different element. [L0037.013]

## Replicating and remixing proven competitor ads

### Core rule: copy the structure, never the words

- Do not copy competitor ad creatives straight from the Meta Ad Library without changes. The competitor's established account history gets preference from Meta, so direct copies do not generate equal reach. [L0037.011]
- When you use a competitor creative as a reference, edit at least one element: the hook, the body copy, or something else that differentiates your version. [L0037.012]
- Imitation means learning from structure and form, not copying word for word. The line between plagiarism and genius is fine, and imitation is a logical learning step before innovation. Great poets imitate and improve; small poets steal and spoil. [L0196.046]
- Competitor ads are the best starting point for your own creative. If they cannot be used, build your own ad from competitor content and improve it rather than copying it. [L0693.043]
- A competitor ad works best as a structure to follow, not a look to copy. Reuse the arrangement of headline, product and offer, and take colours, fonts and brand identity from your own brand. This keeps the test about the structure and avoids using another brand's identity. [L0794.023]
- Look for patterns across several videos, such as a hook or ad copy used repeatedly, and replicate the pattern with your own footage. Do not copy a brand's custom content. For drop-shipping style videos, produce a better version or rearrange existing clips. [L0639.025]
- Use a competitor's idea as a starting point only if you test it yourself. Keep it only if click and result numbers reach your targets; otherwise change the creative or the offer. [L1219.031]
- Copying other dropshippers' creatives is acceptable at the very beginning. In the long run, your own creatives perform better. Ordering the product and filming your own material usually beats reusing other ads. [L1216.019]
- Use a proven line from your Structure Library's Proven Line-Patterns as an example of a psychological move, not as a phrase to repeat. Default to reproducing the move with fresh words. Use a proven line verbatim only if it is genuinely the strongest option, never to avoid the work of writing a fresh version. [L0039.024]
- Competitor creatives can serve as inspiration. Take their images or GIFs, edit them, and improve headlines and angles with editing tools rather than using them unchanged. The aim is a clearly better version than the competitor's ad or landing page. [L0708.056]
- Recreate a viral competitor video by improving its hook or other weak parts, not by copying it. [L0795.025]
- Repurpose existing competitor footage by cutting out their text and logos, changing the brand colours and adding a new narrative. The goal is a different story built on the same footage, not a copy of the original ad. [L0644.028]
- Exact copy-paste is risky. The platform can detect it, and the competitor may get the original ad taken down, which takes your ad down too. Always alter the metadata, logo and details of any replicated creative. [L0398.023]
- Copying a competitor's ads and store exactly can produce high CPM and poor CTR. Change elements such as music, speed, length and hook so Meta does not treat them as duplicates of another advertiser's content. [L1316.032]
- Instead of reusing a brand's ad video, copy its hook or structure and source your own clips from AliExpress, Alibaba or YouTube. This keeps the selling pattern, avoids the brand's content and reduces copyright risk. [L1218.036]

### Sourcing proven creatives

**Where to look and what to save**

- Ripped creatives are videos that already perform for other advertisers. Find them on Kalodata, the TikTok Creative Center or the Facebook Ad Library. Their audience psychology is already proven, which makes them a safe first test. [L1252.004]
- Ad libraries show what creative types work, including posts that go viral. Identify which trends, post types and ad types work, then recreate the winning approach in your own style without copying it. [L1425.004]
- Pool-building: Kalodata lists more than 4,000 video and ad creatives for one product. Use that pool to pull hooks and testimonials and build many variations, not one or two new ads. [L0901.015]
- Content from other products in the same category can serve your product. Eyeliner ads, for example, can supply hooks and testimonials for another eyeliner. This widens your pool well beyond one product's ads. [L0901.014]
- Do not run the same top-performing competitor ads that many advertisers already show on Facebook. The audience has probably seen them. Bring content the market has not seen yet, even when the product is the same. [L0901.003]
- Choose only videos that feature real people. Abstract videos and product-only videos are excluded. [L0704.009]

**Filtering and quantities**

| Source | Filter before saving | Quantity per product | Source ids |
|---|---|---|---|
| Kalodata | High CTR, high spend or proven conversions | At least 20 top videos, whichever filter you use | [L1252.006, L1252.007] |
| TikTok Creative Center or Facebook Ad Library | High CTR, high spend or proven conversions | 3 to 5 top ads; prefer high engagement and many comments | [L1252.006, L1252.008] |
| TikTok Creative Center or Facebook Ad Library, short on time | Filtering can be skipped; go straight to the top-performing ads | 3 to 5 top ads per product | [L1252.024] |

- For every saved video, also save its caption, text overlays, hook and call to action. These are the basis for later comparison. [L1252.009]
- Download only clean versions without a watermark. A watermark shows another account's branding inside your ad. [L1252.011, L1252.021]

**Selection checks**

- Judge each candidate on two checks. The opening hook must grab attention, and the video must show a problem your product actually solves. A video can pass the hook check and still fail the second one, so both checks are needed. [L0704.019]
- Skip a video if the outcome it shows is not the result your product delivers, even when the hook performs well. [L0704.010]
- Filter for high CTR and proven conversions before you test a video in your own account. Recycling earlier ads with the same structure also saves production time. [L1252.006, L1398.002]

### Analysing a winning ad

**Framework for a working ad**

1. Read the hook and check whether it uses the customer's own language. [L0772.034]
2. Identify the awareness stage the ad targets. [L0772.034]
3. Identify the unique mechanism that explains what makes the product different. [L0772.034]
4. Note where the ad sends traffic (product page, advertorial or inverted product page) and what offer is shown. [L0772.034]
5. Check how long the ad has run and how many duplicates use it. [L0772.034]
6. Rebuild the same structure around your own product, changing the words rather than copying the text. [L0772.034]

**Breaking down a video**

- Break each successful competitor creative down every five seconds to identify the hook, the angle and the copywriting. Then write similar copy using the same angle. [L0693.044]
- Study the competitor's ad for the same product: save the videos, review what worked, and copy the structure, text-to-speech and sounds in your own way. This is often more effective than writing a script from scratch. [L1383.051]
- Copy the style of the largest pages or videos for your product, then change it based on what viewers say in the comments and add something dramatic or unusual. Changes that work include new trending sounds, different backdrops, switching between a male and a female presenter, trending video effects, voice-overs and challenge-style framing. [L1367.008]

**Tool for ad analysis**

- Use Facebook Ad Library or Kalodata to find bottom-of-funnel image ads from any competitor in any niche. Screenshot the ad, upload it to Claude, and ask what makes it work and why it is effective, then have Claude create a prompt so you can produce similar ads for your niche. This reverse-engineers winning structures without copying them. [L0316.045]

### Prompts for analysis and recreation

**Analysis prompt for a proven rival video** (send with the video file and the exported brand data; procedure in L0374.033)

```
Here is a proven rival video, sent along with its video file and the brand data I exported. Give me a complete breakdown of why it wins. Go through it frame by frame, and for each moment describe what appears on screen, what is spoken, and what effect that has on the viewer. Give special weight to the hook in the opening seconds and to the individual words and phrases doing the heaviest persuasive work, explaining per frame why each one lands. Using the supplied brand data, identify the persona, the core desire, the emotions in play, the awareness level, the concept, the angle, the USPs, and the offer behind the video. End with a brief list of what to keep and what to modify if this same structure is applied to a different product.
```
[L0374.034]

**Recreation prompt for your own product** (send with the video file, the brand data and your product files)

```
Here is the winning video from my competitor and its exported brand data. Recreate this ad script exactly as it is, keeping the same structure, the same order of scenes, the same timing, the same hook, the same emotional beats and the same length. Replace only the product, its facts, prices, ingredients and claims with those of my product, using only the facts in the attached product files and inventing no new claims. Output the full script for my product, scene by scene.
```
[L0374.035]

**Rewrite prompt for ad copy and product page text**

```
I sell [PRODUCT] in the [NICHE] niche in [MARKET]. Below is the ad copy and product page text of a brand whose ads have been running for a long time: [PASTE AD COPY AND PAGE TEXT]. Rewrite the whole text for my product and keep the same structure, hooks, sections and emotional angle. Write it for this target avatar: [TARGET AVATAR: age, gender, main problem, what they want]. Do not copy any sentence word for word. Avoid medical or guaranteed-result claims and keep all claims within what is allowed for [MARKET]. Return the output in this order: 3 hook variations for ads, 1 primary ad text, 1 headline, then the product page sections in order: hero headline and benefits, testimonials, FAQ.
```
[L1479.017]

**Replicate a proven competitor video (Method 1)**

1. In the Brands tracker, open the brand's top ad from the Ad Copies, Personas or Overview lists. [L0374.033]
2. Click View ad, then download the video. [L0374.033]
3. Generate the transcript with Transcribe ad with AI and copy the full script. [L0374.033]
4. Go back to the brand page and use Export CSV on the tabs to export the brand data (ad copies, hooks, personas, angles, desires, emotions, awareness stages, USPs). [L0374.033]
5. Open Gemini (or Claude), log in, click the plus button and attach the video file. [L0374.033]
6. Attach the exported brand data CSV. [L0374.033]
7. Paste the analysis prompt above and send it. [L0374.033, L0374.034]
8. Attach all files you have for your own product and send the recreation prompt above. [L0374.033, L0374.035]

### Ripping and editing a winning video

**Ripped-creative test (unchanged launch)**

1. Find top-performing videos on Kalodata, the TikTok Creative Center or the Facebook Ad Library, filtering by high CTR, high spend or proven conversions. [L1252.023]
2. Save at least 20 top videos per product if you use Kalodata, or 3 to 5 top ads per product if you use the TikTok Creative Center or the Facebook Ad Library, preferring high engagement plus comments. [L1252.023]
3. Save the captions, text overlays, hooks and CTAs of each video for reference. [L1252.023]
4. Download the clean videos without watermark using Snaptik, ssstik or Downloader Bot. [L1252.023]
5. Upload the videos directly to Meta Ads Manager (TikTok Ads is also possible) without any editing. [L1252.023]
6. Do not change the hook, caption or length; test the product and the offer. [L1252.023]
7. Once you get consistent profitable sales with ripped creatives, begin hook testing to raise CTR. [L1252.023]

- The purpose of the first launch is to test exactly what already works, so do not change the hook, the caption or the video length. [L1252.013]
- Testing ripped videos unchanged isolates whether the product and offer work, because the videos have already been proven with real viewers. [L1252.014]
- Changing the hook, caption or length of a ripped video before the first launch removes the advantage of testing a proven ad. The result no longer shows whether the original works. [L1252.020]
- Case: an operator sold a product using only ripped creatives, with no original content. The proven videos were downloaded without watermark and uploaded unchanged to the ad account. The reported revenue was more than 16,000 USD in a single day from ripped ads alone, which shows that ripped creatives can scale. [L1252.019]

**Remove identifying mentions**

- Remove every spoken or on-screen mention of TikTok Shop from a copied video, and every mention of Orange Cart, before you use it in your ads. [L0704.006]
- For proven videos, remove only the problematic parts. Adding new hooks or heavy edits to a video that already sells can break what works. [L0704.014]

**Ripping and editing a competitor's winning video (method for the Ad Library and TikTok)**

- Save the competitor's video from the Ad Library: open the ad in the Facebook Ad Library, right-click the video and save it to your computer. If the file does not play, change the format to MP4. [L1172.040]
- Download the competitor's current videos, upload them to your Business Manager, and test how they perform for your product. [L1347.015]
