```
13. Tie authority to the claim: link to a respected publication, expert, or award.
14. Show before and after: display the transformation.
15. Stress how new the claim is: present the product as the latest technology.
16. Stress the exclusivity of the claim: be among the first to use it, so the reader feels status.
```

[L0515.019]

**Tactic examples**

- Measure the size: state a specific, measurable result so the reader can judge it. The number makes the claim concrete and easier to believe.
  - Examples: 'Our brush removes 99% of pet hair in one sweep.' 'Cut your monthly grocery spend by 15% with one shared list.' [L0516.038]
- Measure the speed: name a short time frame in which the result happens, so the reader sees how quickly the problem goes away.
  - Examples: 'Say goodbye to pet hair on your furniture in under five minutes.' 'Clear a clogged drain in under two minutes with no chemicals.' [L0516.039]
- Metamorphose the claim: describe the product as a different, vivid object that performs the function in an exaggerated way, which makes the mechanism memorable.
  - Examples: 'This brush is a magnet for every hair on your bed.' 'This mop is a sponge that soaks up spills in a single pass.' [L0516.040]
- Sensitize the claim: attach the reader's senses to the outcome, such as touch, sight or smell, so the benefit feels physical.
  - Examples: 'Imagine running your hand over your couch and feeling nothing but smooth fabric.' 'Picture a kitchen that smells fresh the moment you walk in.' [L0516.041]
- Demonstrate the claim: show a concrete visual scene of the result in a small, specific amount of time, so the reader can picture the proof.
  - Examples: 'See a month of dust lifted from a single sofa cushion in one pass.' 'Watch one swipe collect all the crumbs from a car seat.' [L0516.042]
- New mechanism question: name the unique mechanism, add curiosity, and tie it to the problem outcome in the form 'Could [new mechanism] really [outcome]?' Keep the mechanism in the headline so the reader sees what makes the product different.
  - Examples: 'Could this heated insole really end cold feet on early morning runs?' 'Could a single tap really lift every stain from your sofa?' [L0516.043]

**Objection and benefit headlines**

- Turn the biggest objection into the headline: name it openly, then explain why it is a benefit.
  - Example one: Not the lightest bag on the market, because it's built to carry a laptop and a week of groceries without tearing.
  - Example two: Not cheap, and we're fine with that, because it lasts through years of daily use. [L0378.064]
- Benefit-led headline: name the outcome the buyer wants in their own words, then the product quietly solves the underlying problem.
  - Example one: Get your old routine back, and stop wasting evenings on the wrong fix.
  - Example two: Get the weekend you were promised, and leave the chores to a system that already runs itself. [L0378.075]

**The 38 ways to strengthen a headline**

Thirty-eight ways to strengthen a headline by how the claim is worded, in the original order:

1. Measure the size of the claim with an exact number.
2. Measure the speed of the claim with a time figure.
3. Compare the claim against a rival, a higher price or an older method.
4. Express the claim as a metaphor.
5. Make the reader feel, smell, taste, touch, see or hear the claim.
6. Demonstrate the claim with one prime example.
7. Dramatize the claim or its result as a short scene.
8. State the claim as a paradox.
9. Remove a usual limitation from the claim.
10. Attach the claim to a value or a person the prospect wants to be like.
11. Show in detail how much work the claim does.
12. State the claim as a question.
13. Offer information on how to get the result.
14. Attach an authority to the claim.
15. Use a before-and-after contrast.
16. Stress that the claim is new.
17. Stress that the claim is exclusive to you.
18. Turn the claim into a challenge the reader can test.
19. Present the claim as a short first-person case statement.
20. Condense the claim by naming your product as the replacement for the old one.
21. Symbolize the claim with a parallel image instead of a direct measure.
22. Connect the mechanism to the claim inside the headline.
23. Startle the reader by contradicting how he thinks the mechanism works.
24. Connect the need and the claim in one line.
25. Offer information inside the ad as the hook.
26. Turn the claim or the need into a short case story.
27. Name the problem or need precisely.
28. Warn the reader about the risks of not using the product.
29. Emphasize the claim through phrasing, by splitting it into two sentences or repeating part of it.
30. Show the claim is easy by pointing to a limit everyone already accepts as overcome.
31. State the difference that sets the product apart.
32. Surprise the reader into seeing that a former limit no longer applies.
33. Address the people who cannot buy the product.
34. Address the prospect directly by the role or rank he holds.
35. Dramatize how hard it was to make the product.
36. Say the claim sounds too good, to meet the reader's doubt head-on.
37. Challenge the prospect's limiting belief about himself.
38. Turn the claim into a question and answer it.

[L0330.096]

### Crowded markets and unique features

- Crowded-market headline: name the unique feature in the headline when many similar products already exist. The feature is the hook.
  - Example: 'Unique microfiber static head removes more hair than any other brush' [L0353.041]
- Name the unique mechanism or feature so the buyer can tell the product apart. The pattern names a unique mechanism, a concrete result and a short time frame.
  - Examples: 'Patented magnetic head pulls hair out of every fabric in one pass.' 'Dual-layer cleaning pad lifts pet fur from sofas in seconds.' [L0353.042]

### Lead types

**Choosing the lead: direct or indirect**

- The more aware and ready the prospect, the more direct the lead should be. The less aware or more skeptical the prospect, the more indirect the lead should be. Direct leads fail when the audience is skeptical or does not yet believe a solution exists. [L0756.006]
- Direct approaches work well when the product is easy to understand, the promise is large but easily accepted, the deal or guarantee is exceptional, the customer already trusts the seller, or a product improvement was already awaited by the market. [L0756.007]
- Indirect approaches work better when the customer knows little about the seller, the product needs explanation, the customer is jaded and skeptical, a timely news connection is strong, or the product is being reinvented or elevated. [L0756.008]
- Being clever or coy is not the same as being indirect. A lead that entertains without ever connecting to the product often leaves the prospect unclear about what is being sold. [L0756.009]
- A direct lead with a skeptical or highly aware-but-jaded prospect, such as a car buyer or someone who has heard too many similar offers, usually fails. Shift toward the indirect side to rebuild trust first. [L0756.010]

**Promise lead**

- Use the Promise Lead for prospects who are mostly aware and almost ready to buy, and for prospects sitting on the fence. It opens with the product's biggest and most relevant claim and usually ties the claim to a core desire. [L0756.027]
- A Promise Lead must target the prospect's core desire. The promise should be original, relevant, bold but believable, and supported by proof at least as strong as the claim. Oversized promises that cannot be proven make skeptics disbelieve the whole message. [L0756.028]
- To find a strong promise: first check what competitors have already promised, then identify what the prospect expects, and finally identify what the product can truly deliver without overselling. Under-delivery from an over-sold product makes the product fail faster. [L0756.029]
- When a promise seems too large and readers become skeptical, reduce the claim, turn it into a question that addresses the doubt, or shrink it to a believable size. Scaling a claim back can make it more credible, as a Sears battery demonstration with three or four cars was more believable than one with ten. [L0756.032]
- Promise lead pattern: state the product's biggest benefit as the headline, add a specific time frame or result, then prove it.
  - Formula: '[Desired result] in [short time frame], without [common objection].'
  - New example: 'Clear, even skin in 14 days, without the redness that harsher serums cause.'
  - New example: 'Sleep through the night in one week, with no sleep aids or alarms needed.'
  - The time frame makes the promise concrete, and the second clause pre-empts the common objection. [L0756.033]
- Promise leads usually fail with skeptics and highly unaware prospects, because a bare promise sounds like one more sales claim. They work best with people on the fence who just need a nudge. [L0756.034]

**Problem-solution lead**

- Show empathy first, linger on the problem only long enough to earn a commitment to read on, then offer hope of a relevant solution. Lingering too long without offering hope makes the copy feel like it exploits fear. [L0756.036]
- Name the deep emotional worry in one phrase (for example guilt, shame, fear of running out of money), then offer relief.
  - Formula: '[Painful situation]? Here is what ends it.'
  - New example: 'Worried your savings won't last past 75? Here is how to build a withdrawal plan that keeps paying out.'
  - New example: 'Tired of feeling like the only one who can't keep up at work? Here is a 10-minute routine that closes the gap.'
  - It works because it names the feeling and immediately gives a path to relief. [L0756.037]

**Question and inversion leads**

- Questions that state a problem with an almost inevitable yes answer from the right audience are a strong way to start a conversation. The word 'these' in a question like 'Do You Make These Mistakes?' can make the problem feel like it applies to the reader personally. [L0756.040]
- Inversion (solution-problem): promise the benefit of escaping or avoiding a situation before naming the problem.
  - Formula: 'Enjoy [benefit] without [problem].'
  - New example: 'Keep your savings growing without the stress of market swings.'
  - New example: 'Get the energy you need for your day without the afternoon crash.'
  - The reader senses the solution first, and the problem is framed as something they can avoid. [L0756.041]

**Invented-term problem**

- Give the problem a new name that makes sense of the negative situation, then explain it so the reader learns what it means and what to do about it.
  - Formula: '[Coined term]: Is it costing you [specific loss]?'
  - New example: 'Pantry drift: Is it quietly adding $40 a month to your grocery bill?'
  - New example: 'Comparison fatigue: Is it making your savings feel smaller than they are?'
  - A new label feels like insider knowledge and creates curiosity about the cure. [L0756.042]

**Invitation lead**

- Frame the offer as an exclusive membership or invitation so the prospect feels included, and reveal the deal details less openly. It works for products with a long tradition of quality, clubs, societies and luxury items, but only when the offer really has exclusive value.
  - Pattern: 'You are invited to join [exclusive group] and receive [valuable access] before anyone else.'
  - New example: 'You are invited to join the Alpine Pantry Circle, where members receive first access to limited-batch olive oil each season.'
  - Exclusion creates desire to be let in. [L0756.025]

**Secret lead**

- Use a Secret Lead when a product has an element the customer does not know, or when its known qualities can be renamed or reframed to feel new. Start the secret in the headline and keep the teaser going through the copy. [L0756.043]
- The secret must be both intriguing and beneficial, and tied to a major benefit of the product quickly enough that the reader understands why the secret matters. [L0756.044]
- Do not disclose the secret during the lead. Revealing it too soon removes the curiosity that keeps the prospect reading. For many Secret Leads, the secret is held back until the prospect buys the product. [L0756.045]
- Specificity overcomes the skepticism that secrets trigger. Exact figures, dates, named sources and worked examples make a teaser feel credible even when the secret is not yet explained. [L0756.046]
- Provide clues as the copy progresses: restate the headline in different words, add dates, name credible figures or celebrities, or tell the reader what the secret is not. The prospect feels closer to the answer while the actual answer stays hidden. [L0756.047]
- Secret lead pattern: a headline combining a credible claim with an unexplained term, a number, or a closed-then-reopened opportunity, with the secret deferred to the body copy.
  - Formula: '[Unfamiliar term] That [specific result] for [specific investment]'
  - New example: 'The Harvest Ledger Method That Turned a $200 Pantry Budget Into $1,800 in Savings.'
  - New example: 'The Quiet Lever Behind Consistent 9-Minute Morning Routines That Actually Stick.'
  - The reader must read on to learn what the term means and how the result was achieved. [L0756.048]
- Transubstantiation means taking something ordinary and reframing it as something special, carrying over the emotional appeal of a more exciting example. Neologizing means giving a familiar concept a new name to create intrigue. Use one of these when the product's qualities are already known. [L0756.049]

**Proclamation lead**

- A Proclamation Lead opens with a bold, emotionally compelling statement that is relevant and nearly unbelievable, usually in the headline. The copy then provides evidence that makes the implied promise believable, and the product is revealed only after the proof is shown. [L0756.050]
- Use it for consumer products when the prospect is unaware of the product, and for business-to-business audiences already aware of the product who could be alarmed by a fact that threatens their current tools or practices. [L0756.051]
- Proclamation pattern: an imperative or declarative headline implying a serious consequence, followed by a claim the reader wants to check.
  - Formula: '[Imperative] or [consequence]' or '[Outdated tool] Is Obsolete.'
  - New example: 'Stop Using Your Old Budget Sheet. It Is Costing You Up to 30% More Than You Realize.'
  - New example: 'Your 2019 Shipping Calculator Is Obsolete: Here Is What Changed in Carrier Rates.'
  - It startles, creates a worry about the status quo, and promises a clear way forward. [L0756.052]

### Editorial and advertorial headlines

- Editorial headlines should be benefit-driven, combining a news-style or attention-grabbing claim with a benefit or curiosity element. A plain product name or price in the headline weakens the editorial. [L0578.015]
- Headline pattern: pair a surprising problem or bold claim with a benefit or curiosity hook, such as a benefit-driven news headline or an expert reveal. The headline decides whether the reader continues, so it must be interesting enough to keep them on the page.
  - Example 1: 'Why Millions of Commuters Wake Up Stiff and the Surprising Pillow Fix Experts Recommend'
  - Example 2: 'Vet Reveals the Simple Daily Habit That Keeps Dogs Moving Well Into Their Senior Years' [L0578.013]
- Numbered advertorial headline: [number] reasons [target audience] [keeps failing at, or is missing out on, a specific problem], [promised fix or time frame]. The number signals a quick, scannable read, and naming a specific problem lets the reader see themselves in it before the product appears.
  - Example: 'Four reasons your sourdough keeps collapsing, and the fix takes one weekend.'
  - Example 2: 'Three mistakes most home office workers make with desk lighting, and how to fix each in minutes.' [L0552.049]

### Meta titles and descriptions

- The meta description and headline are the ad for an article in Google search results, so they must sell the click. Use persuasive sales copy in these fields, which is a different skill from writing article body text. [L0382.031]
- Headline and meta description formula: name the exact topic people search for, add a concrete benefit or a question the searcher wants answered, then add a credibility cue such as the brand or a specific detail. Search results are ads that must win a click against competitors, so the searcher should see that the page answers their exact need.
  - Example 1 (new): Shopify vs. WooCommerce: Which Platform Fits a $5,000 Monthly Budget?
  - Example 2 (new): Should an Online Store Show a Phone Number? What Shoppers Expect in 2026 [L0382.033]

### Other title patterns

- Personalised gift-book titles: replace a generic title with a short phrase about the relationship between the giver and the recipient, such as what they share or how they feel about each other. Keep it short enough for the cover.
  - New examples: 'Two Hearts, One Shared Story' and 'Counting Every Reason, Twice' [L0333.006]

### Testing headlines

- Signs and headlines do not need to be artistic, but they must say the right thing. Test variations until a clear winner appears. [L0378.077]
- A fruit stand split-tested signs and found that a short, direct line such as 'Picked Today' outperformed more generic phrases. Daily income rose from hundreds of dollars to more than $1,000 with the winning sign. [L0378.076]
- Check each headline device against three jobs. A device should do at least one of these: strengthen the claim with more detail or measurement, make a familiar claim fresh by changing its angle, or pull the reader into the body copy by promising information or asking a question. A device that does none of these adds nothing. [L0330.097]

### Headline Principles

- A headline selects the people who could be interested and speaks to them directly, so the reader can tell at a glance whether the ad concerns them. Write each headline for one specific audience, not for everyone. [L1261.055]
- Clever, blind, or amusing headlines may attract many more people, but most are not buyers, so the ad's true response falls. Headlines that hide the offer or product do not reach the right people. [L1261.056]
- The headline has the largest effect on return. The same ad body run with different headlines can differ by five to ten times in response. Test several headlines against the same body copy and keep the one with the best cost per customer. [L1261.057]
- One advertiser's keyed record for a single product included nearly two thousand headlines, and results varied enormously even when the body copy was almost identical. Headline testing is worth the effort. [L1261.058]
- A headline counts as copy because its only job is to persuade the reader to continue with the rest of the content. The same headline principles apply to blog posts and similar content, although general educational content writing is a separate discipline. *(Older: source 2021-22.)* [L1460.009]
- In a letter, headlines do most of the selling, so they must be as strong as a print ad headline. Place the headline above the salutation or between the salutation and body, in bold or a boxed panel, because it gets the reader past the first glance. [L1370.020]
- The main headline of a page should be bold and clearly visible, at most one to two lines. It can be a USP, a bold claim about the product, or a benefit-driven statement placed in the first section of the page. [L0916.006]
- Open a landing page with a large, bold headline that states the main benefit or desired outcome. Visitors move toward pleasant outcomes and away from painful ones, so the headline should show the gain first. [L1207.002]

### The Four U's

- A headline must carry a lot of information early, because most readers never read beyond it. Its purpose is to grab attention and convey the Four U's: Urgent, Unique, Useful, and Ultra-Specific. The four do not all need to be present, but if two or more are missing, the headline will likely fail to hold attention. [L1356.020]
- **Urgent:** Usually conveyed by a date or time-limited prompt, such as *Take action by December 21* or *Sale ends this Friday*, or indirectly through FOMO when the big emotion is strong. Urgency is the simplest U and can be dropped if the other three are present. [L1356.021]
- **Unique:** Non-negotiable. The headline must offer something the reader has never seen before. To find a unique angle, pick one specific element of the product or offer and emphasize it, such as a feature competitors do not highlight or a fresh framing. The revolution is not required; the unique element can be small, as long as the reader has not seen it. [L1356.023]
- **Useful:** The headline must promise something the audience values. Research the ideal prospect, what topics they are currently curious about, and which benefits would make them keep reading. A headline built only on intrigue is not useful and fails the "What's in it for me?" test. [L1356.024]
- **Useful, tied to a hot topic:** Tie the useful promise to a topic top of mind for the audience, such as a major news event or government policy, then add a concrete, useful benefit such as a money figure. The topic creates interest and the benefit creates usefulness. [L1356.025]
- **Ultra-Specific:** Use uncommon, oddly precise numbers rather than round figures, for example $10,251 instead of $10,000, 12.5 years younger instead of 10, or a 251% strength gain instead of 100%. Precise numbers imply the claim was tested and make it seem real. Be as specific as legally possible and do not lie. Ideally, the specific figure is backed by an example demonstrated in the lead or body. [L1356.022]

### Specificity and Numbers

- Specific measured claims beat general superlatives, because readers assume a precise figure reflects a real test. Formula: state the measured result, the test size or method behind it, and the concrete benefit. [L1261.059]
  - *Stops pain in 30 seconds, measured on 400 users.* [L1261.059]
  - *Cuts drying time by 42 percent versus the leading brand.* [L1261.059]
- Pattern: a specific number from a real test or process turns a common claim into a fact that stands apart from rivals. Formula: name the common benefit, then add the exact figure that proves it. [L1261.080]
  - *Lasts 9 hours on a single charge, tested across 60 days of use.* [L1261.080]
  - *Sets in 12 seconds, measured on 200 test batches.* [L1261.080]
- Solution-first property headline: *How to Do Wonders With a Little Land!* beat a conventional problem-solution headline by 40%. It also beat a flat promise headline, *Two Acres and Security*, by 75%. Start with the solution when the reader's problem is familiar and the product is clearly relevant. [L0756.071]
- Problem-solution campaigns can also work at scale. In the Kimberly-Clark case below, they helped build a brand worth $1.6 billion, so the choice between problem-first and solution-first depends on whether the reader already knows the problem and sees the product as relevant. [L0756.067, L0756.071]

### Finding the Angle

- Concept headline from a production detail: a technical detail that explains why a product is special can become the headline concept. Ask the manufacturer how a feature is made and why competitors cannot copy it, since that answer often holds the strongest angle. Example: *Laser Beam Digital Watch* came from learning that the laser was the only way to seal the capsule. [L1366.083]
- Curiosity from an unusual but true fact about how the product works invites the reader to learn more. Formula: state a surprising fact, then reveal the mechanism or benefit that explains it. [L1261.081]
  - *Your morning coffee gives its kick two hours after you drink it.* [L1261.081]
  - *Each batch is filtered through a material that catches particles smaller than a human hair.* [L1261.081]
- Question about a surprising, specific unknown tied to the reader's trade or daily life. The reader must read the first line to get the answer. An unanswered question creates curiosity, and relevance to the reader's work keeps it from being mere entertainment. [L1369.117]
  - *What is the one invoice error that quietly drains a small shop's cash every month?* [L1369.117]
  - *Why do some restaurants keep their regulars for ten years while others lose them after a single visit?* [L1369.117]

### Benefit Headline Formulas

- Pattern: [desired outcome] + [novelty word] + [low-effort or fun word]. It promises the goal while removing the perceived effort and sacrifice. [L1207.004]
  - *The simple new way to sleep through the night.* [L1207.004]
  - *The fun way to keep your dog active every day.* [L1207.004]
- Headline formula: combine the big desired outcome with a novelty word that signals something different from what the buyer already tried and failed, and an effort-reducing word that signals it is quick or easy. [L1209.003]
  - *The fresh and easy way to build strength at home.* [L1209.003]
  - *The smarter way to learn a language in 10 minutes a day.* [L1209.003]
- Principle: novelty words such as "new" make an offer feel different from failed past attempts, which raises interest. Effort-reducing words such as "fun" or "easy" counter the common belief that reaching a goal is resource-intensive, slow, or unpleasant. Benefit headlines work best when they signal low effort. [L1207.003, L1209.004]
- Pattern: [product] suitable for [broad group], [skill or experience] not required. It removes the fear of not being good enough. [L1207.012]
  - *Built for beginners and pros alike, no training required.* [L1207.012]
  - *Works for every shoe size, no tools needed.* [L1207.012]
- Formula: [Specific measurable outcome] in [timeframe] [without the usual cost, effort, or risk]. A concrete outcome with a timeframe makes the big promise believable, and naming what is avoided removes the main objection. [L1365.014]
  - *Cut your monthly grocery bill by $300 within six weeks without clipping coupons or changing what you eat.* [L1365.014]
  - *Earn a second income of $2,500 a month from a phone and a laptop, without building a website or holding inventory.* [L1365.014]
- Formula: Introduce a new [type of solution] that [unique claim] before [the point the market usually waits for]. The "new" element triggers attention, and the unique claim signals a breakthrough the reader has not seen before. [L1365.013]
  - *A new bookkeeping method that flags tax deadlines a full month before your accountant does.* [L1365.013]
  - *A new breathing routine that lowers resting heart rate within ten days without setting foot in a gym.* [L1365.013]
- Product-page pattern: product name, then a USP or bold claim, then the emotional result the buyer gets. The page continues the feeling the ad created, so visitors do not lose the thread of their buying journey. [L0916.007]
  - *Lightweight Standing Desk Mat: Stand for hours without the ache in your lower back.* [L0916.007]
  - *Compact Travel Blender: Fresh smoothies on the road, zero mess in your bag.* [L0916.007]
- Add a short semi-headline or benefit line directly after the product name that uses the same emotion as the ad creative. This keeps the visitor's experience consistent from ad to landing page. [L0916.008]

### Product Image and Customer Language

- Strong product image headlines borrow the words customers use in their reviews, such as the transformation they describe or the frustration they are relieved to be rid of. Formula: real customer phrase plus the outcome it promises, short enough to read at a glance. [L0887.026]
  - *Finally sleep through the night without waking up sore.* (transformation) [L0887.026]
  - *No more scrubbing the stains off by hand.* (removed frustration) [L0887.026]
- Transformation headline: Product that takes you from [current pain] to [desired state], often followed by a short pair of outcomes. The reader sees their own pain first, then the before-and-after shift the product promises. [L1164.059]
  - *Running shoes that take you from sore heels to pain-free miles.* [L1164.059]
  - *Coffee that takes you from groggy mornings to focused, steady starts.* [L1164.059]

### Audience and Identification

- Pattern: a headline that names the specific group a product is for signals relevance and filters out everyone else. Formula: state the group, the core benefit for that group, and a concrete result. [L1261.061]
  - *For busy parents: dinner ready in 15 minutes.* [L1261.061]
  - *For runners with knee pain: a sleeve that adds support on every mile.* [L1261.061]
- Identification headlines address the reader as the person who has the problem or is responsible for it. In one comparison, a headline naming the older-looking woman beat a solution-only headline by a large margin, because it targeted a feeling she wanted removed. Formula: *For the [person] Who [problem they feel or cause].* [L0756.066]
  - *For the Freelancer Who Chases Invoices Every Month.* [L0756.066]
  - *For the Homeowner Who Keeps Paying for Repairs That Should Have Been Caught Early.* [L0756.066]
- Flagged how-to headlines: a straightforward promise of a desirable result, often preceded by a flag that names the specific reader. This makes the headline feel written for the reader. [L1370.024]
  - *How To Get Your First Ten Reviews In Two Weeks.* [L1370.024]
  - *For Freelancers Who Hate Invoicing: How To Get Paid On Time.* [L1370.024]
- Question and conditional headlines: a question that challenges or provokes the reader, or an "If you are X, you can Y" statement that targets the reader's identity. [L1370.025]
  - *Are You Losing Sales Because Your Photos Look Cheap?* [L1370.025]
  - *If You Are Over 50, You Can Still Start a Profitable Online Store.* [L1370.025]

### Lead Types

- Offer and promise elements can be combined with other lead types, because every sales piece needs them anyway. Most other combinations break the one-idea focus. A secret lead can be paired with a promise, for example a technique kept hidden while the headline promises a result, as long as one idea and one emotion drive the copy. [L0756.062]
- **Secret lead:** In a typical secret lead, around 300 to 400 words go to illustrating the promise and building credibility before the secret is named. The secret itself stays withheld until the reader is emotionally ready to buy. [L0756.063]
- **Story lead:** Testimonials, founder or expert bios, historical proof, and track records can all serve as the basis of a story lead. Story leads engage readers who do not know the seller or who distrust bold claims. Tell the story quickly and tie it back to the core promise of the promotion. A story lead can work directly or indirectly, depending on the audience. [L0756.064]
- **Indirect story opener:** Describe two people who start from the same background and end up in different situations, with no product or offer mentioned until later. The reader keeps going to learn why the paths split, and the sale follows once interest and emotion are set. Pattern: *Two [people with same starting point] began the same way; one [outcome A], one [outcome B].* [L0756.065]
  - *Two freelance designers signed their first client on the same week; one now sets her own rates, the other still waits for invoices to clear.* [L0756.065]
  - *Two neighbors bought the same model of rain barrel; one has a full garden tank every summer, the other has a rusted lid and an empty yard.* [L0756.065]
  - This works because the reader wants to know the cause of the difference, and the product becomes the answer. [L0756.065]
- Underdog story headline: says someone was doubted for attempting something and then succeeded. It appeals to sympathy for the underdog and to the reader's own private doubts. [L1370.021]
  - *They Said My Small Shop Would Never Last Past Winter, and It Just Hit Its Best Year.* [L1370.021]
  - *Everyone Laughed When I Asked for a Raise. Here Is What Happened Next.* [L1370.021]
- Who-else headline: a question or statement that implies many other people already know something the reader does not, creating curiosity and fear of missing out. [L1370.022]
  - *Who Else Wants Their Kitchen Clean Without Scrubbing?* [L1370.022]
  - *Who Else Is Quietly Cutting Their Shipping Bill in Half?* [L1370.022]
- First-person story headline: starts with how something changed for the writer, followed by a dramatic result. It works best when the before and after are very different and the story has real stakes. [L1370.023]
  - *How a Cheap Tripod Turned My Sales Around in One Month.* [L1370.023]
  - *How I Doubled My Repeat Customers Without Spending a Cent on Ads.* [L1370.023]
- Secrets, numbers, and warnings: "Secrets of" headlines promise insider knowledge, "N Ways to" headlines add a specific number to a how-to promise, and "Warning:" headlines grab attention for problem-solution copy. [L1370.026]
  - *Secrets of Shops That Sell Out Every Monday.* [L1370.026]
  - *17 Ways to Cut Your Packaging Costs.* [L1370.026]
  - *Warning: Your Current Supplier May Be Adding Hidden Fees.* [L1370.026]
- Promise and crowd headlines: "Give me X and I will Y" telegraphs a clear, short offer, and "Thousands now do X even though they Y" uses a crowd plus a surprising contrast to build belief. [L1370.027]
  - *Give Me Ten Minutes a Day and I Will Show You How to Automate Your Orders.* [L1370.027]
  - *Thousands Now Sell Online Even Though They Never Studied Business.* [L1370.027]
- Promise-only check: remove the offer, price, and guarantee from the headline or opening promise, then read the bare promise. [L0756.073]
  1. Take the headline or opening promise and remove the offer, price, and guarantee.
  2. Read the bare promise and decide whether it still creates anticipation.
  3. If it does, use it as the opening for prospects who are on the fence or not ready for an offer yet.
  4. If it does not, make the promise more specific or more relevant to the core desire. [L0756.073]
- Indirect leads carry specific risks: using an indirect angle when a direct offer would have worked, choosing an angle too subtle to connect back to the product, taking so long to reach the product that the reader gets bored, and writing something interesting that has nothing to do with the sale. Clever or coy copy that never ties to the product is not indirect selling and often leaves the prospect unclear about what is for sale. [L0756.074]

### Offer and Sale Headlines

- Sale headline formula that converts for a specific customer: use a short line that speaks to the customer's situation or the moment they are in, then put the offer in a badge or subheading. It works better than generic sale slogans because it tells the reader the offer is meant for them. [L0992.018]
  - *Chilly commutes need a better layer. Get 40% off until Sunday.* [L0992.018]
  - *Old sneakers holding you back? Your new pair is 25% off this week.* [L0992.018]
- Service-first offer: tell a trial or sample story instead of asking for a purchase, because it lowers the reader's risk. Formula: state the free or low-risk benefit, the way to get it, and what the buyer keeps. [L1261.060]
  - *Try a full week of the new filter at home before you pay a cent.* [L1261.060]
  - *Get a free sample pack of our blend at your nearest store, no purchase needed.* [L1261.060]
- Returning-visitor offer headlines: address the visitor as returning, state a concrete discount or benefit, and put it in the headline to raise click-through rate. Original forms were *Special offer for returning visitors* and *Returning visitors get 10% off*. [L1203.022]
  - *Welcome back: free shipping on your cart today.* [L1203.022]
  - *Returning visitors save 15% this week.* [L1203.022]

### Advertorial and Pre-sales Headlines

- Advertorial headlines work when they promise practical, specific knowledge about a problem the reader already has, framed as education rather than an ad. Formula: a credible insider angle + a specific symptom or problem + a concrete benefit or secret to learn. [L1131.058]
  - *Why senior dogs lose their walking energy, and the three daily habits that help them feel younger again.* [L1131.058]
  - *Five overlooked reasons a cat's coat turns dull, and what owners can check this week.* [L1131.058]
- Pre-sales content titles answer a question the reader already has about a product, such as "Do X really work?", "What to look for in a Y", "The definitive guide to Z", or "The origin of a product". Such titles are engaging enough to get a click from cold traffic. [L1203.033]
  - *Does a magnesium spray really help you sleep?* [L1203.033]
  - *What to look for in a weighted blanket.* [L1203.033]

### Search Listicle Headlines

- Listicle formula: [Number] + [best/top] + [item] + [location or topic] + [audience or experience qualifier]. The base phrase captures the broad search, and the trailing qualifier targets a specific segment such as beginners, advanced users, or first-time buyers without losing general appeal. *(Older: source 2021-22.)* [L1421.031]
  - *11 Best Hiking Trails in Colorado for Every Fitness Level.* (travel niche) [L1421.031]
  - *19 Best Budget Apps for Freelancers Who Are Just Starting Out.* (finance niche) [L1421.031]

### Long-form Sales Headline Blocks

- A long-form sales headline block usually has three parts: a short label line above the headline that signals a limit or warning, the main headline, and a sub-line beneath it that expands the claim with a figure or time frame. A testimonial box is often placed under this block as an extra trust signal. Test the whole block as one unit, since the parts work together. [L1356.071]

### Testing and Adapting Headlines

- Take a printed article, headline list, or product description. [L1343.036]
  1. Use a permanent marker to black out every word you do not want.
  2. Read the remaining words in order; they form a new headline, hook, or short piece of copy.
  3. Adapt the result to your product and audience. [L1343.036]
- Test several headlines against the same body copy and compare cost per customer, not clicks, because clever headlines can draw many non-buyers. [L1261.056, L1261.057]

### Case Studies

- **Kimberly-Clark and Kleenex:** Kimberly-Clark had warehouses of cellucotton, a filter material originally made for gas masks, at the end of World War I. The company first sold Kleenex as a disposable replacement for towels used to remove cold cream. A 1925 magazine campaign promised no more dingy cold-cream towels, using celebrities to say it was how movie stars kept a pretty skin. Other ads tested uses such as handkerchiefs, coffee filters, and cleanup towels. A head researcher with chronic hay fever pushed the top copywriter to rewrite the ads with the handkerchief use up front, under headlines such as *Don't Put a Cold In Your Pocket* and *No more sore noses*. These problem-solution campaigns helped build a brand worth $1.6 billion. [L0756.067]
- **Victor Schwab and the self-help book:** A self-help book was first printed with only 5,000 copies, and its author had a long, unrelated career in sales before teaching the course that became the book. A promise-led space ad by copywriter Victor Schwab used the book's own title promise, followed by a quote and a list of promise-laden chapter titles. This ad and others that followed sold over 15 million copies. [L0756.070]

## Hooks and openings

### What the opening has to do

- A hook is the opening line in the first 1-3 seconds of a video. It stops the scroll and starts a full watch. It works by triggering one of seven psychological patterns, and it decides whether the algorithm sees a watch completion or an exit. [L0160.001]
- The seven triggers are: direct problem relevance, comparison against current solutions, personal authority from experience, curiosity about outcomes, fear of missing out, daily necessity, and removal of cost barriers. [L0160.001]
- The hook is arguably the most important ad element. It must stop the scroll and keep the viewer watching, and it should highlight a fact, a problem, the key benefit or the unique selling point. [L1425.006]
- The first 3 to 5 seconds decide whether a viewer keeps watching. If the hook fails, nobody sees the rest of the ad, however good the offer. [L0707.007, L0777.004]
- The first seconds must stop the scroll and show what the product does right away. Shocking, unexpected or user-generated content (UGC) can achieve this. [L0777.004]
- Attention is only the first step. The opening must also win interest, or attention fades and is much harder to win back. [L1369.040]
- A strong opening drives the click, not only views beyond the hook. [L0950.040]
- A strong ad calls out a problem or a big benefit in the first seconds, so viewers are already qualified buyers. Attention-grabbing content that has no relation to the product attracts viewers who will not buy. [L0640.020]
- A hook should relate to the product, the video and the viewer's own situation, and appeal to emotion. Statements viewers can instantly relate to hold attention longer and improve conversion. [L0764.008]
- Name the audience directly in hooks and copy, for example the profession or life situation. People outside the group keep scrolling, people inside it qualify themselves, and clicks are filtered toward likely buyers. [L1426.044]
- The first three seconds should target one specific audience and show either the pain point or the relief. The right people stay and others skip the ad. [L0871.062]
- Simple copy with a clear hook in the first seconds matters most, because the opening seconds decide whether viewers keep watching. [L1176.038]

### Timing windows

Sources give different time values. Each value applies to a different element of the opening.

| Element | Value | When it applies | Sources |
|---|---|---|---|
| Hook line, length | 1-3 seconds, ideally 1.5-2 seconds | The hook sentence or on-screen hook itself | L0764.006, L0160.001 |
| Hook placement | Within the first 2-3 seconds, early and fast, never in the middle or after 3 seconds | Where the hook must appear | L0764.005 |
| Opening window | First 3-5 seconds | The full hook period, tested as one unit: problem, face or first proof | L0902.018, L0280.016, L0638.035, L0648.057, L0902.017 |
| Problem intro | Keep it short | Before the solution appears | L0640.048 |
| Solution or benefit | Within about 3-5 seconds | Reach the benefit or solution inside this window | L0640.048, L0067.021 |
| Product on screen | Within the first five seconds | Unless the video is a strong unboxing | L1377.021 |
| Offer on screen (TikTok) | Within the first three seconds | So the audience recognises that a product is being sold | L1177.027 |
| Demonstration (video ads) | First three seconds show how the product works, then installation or use | Video ads that lead with the product | L0562.032 |

- The hook must appear within the first 2 to 3 seconds of the video. [L0764.005]
- A hook lasts 1 to 3 seconds, ideally 1.5 to 2 seconds. [L0764.006]
- The first 3 to 5 seconds are the hook. Test that window separately from the rest of the video. [L0902.018]
- The first 3 to 5 seconds should show the pain point, the face or the problem, and then introduce the product. [L0638.035]
- Reach the solution within about 3 to 5 seconds. A product introduction that takes around 10 seconds loses viewers before the benefit appears. [L0640.048]
- If an ad takes 10 seconds or more to introduce the product, jump straight to demonstrating the benefit (the action) within 3 to 5 seconds, then introduce the product. [L0067.021]
- Show the product in the first five seconds. Videos that delay the product tend to underperform unless they are strong unboxings. This applies to custom and sourced content. [L1377.021]
- On TikTok, show the offer within the first three seconds, because the audience needs to recognise a product is being sold, otherwise attention drops. [L1177.027]
- For video ads, the first three seconds must show how the product works as the attention grabber. After those three seconds, show how it is installed or used. [L0562.032]

### Problem first or product first

Sources disagree on what the first frame should show.

- **Problem first:** Show the problem the product solves, not its features or specifications. Do not lead with features such as "battery lasts 3 hours" or "rechargeable". Show the dirty lawn first, then the clean lawn, so customers understand how the product helps. [L0280.016, L0280.017]
- **Problem first, for problem-solving products:** Bold claims and pain points are the most useful for product-led ads. The first seconds should show the audience's problem, the face, or the problem before the product appears. [L0398.010, L0638.035]
- **Result or demonstration first:** Show the working product in the first three seconds (video ads), or show what the product does right away. [L0562.032, L0777.004]
- **Product in first five seconds:** Delayed products tend to underperform unless the video is a strong unboxing. [L1377.021]
- **Use the problem or the demonstration:** Both are valid. Apply the problem-first rule to features-heavy or problem-led products, and the demonstration rule when the video is a product demo. The sources give no further conditions beyond the 10-second rule in L0067.021 and the unboxing exception in L1377.021. [L0280.017, L0562.032, L1377.021, L0067.021]

### Hook categories and choosing one

- Three common hook categories work for Facebook video: [L0398.010]

| Category | What it does | Best use |
|---|---|---|
| Bold claim | A direct, specific statement about the product (long proven) | Product-led ads |
| Pain point | Shows the problem the audience has | Problem-solving products |
| Suspense | Builds curiosity and entertains the right audience at once (TikTok-style) | Short-form feeds |

- Bold claims and pain points are the most useful for product-led ads. Suspense is strong for short-form feeds. [L0398.010]
- Classify each hook by the 13-pattern set. [L0613.012]
  1. Claim size (for example an exact monthly income figure)
  2. Claim speed (a fast result)
  3. Authority figure
  4. Before-and-after
  5. Comparison to rivals
  6. Removal of limitations (for example "even if you have no experience")
  7. Question
  8. Information offer
  9. Newness
  10. Exclusivity
  11. Belief challenge
  12. Direct call-out to a specific person
  13. Identity-based hook
  [L0613.012]

### Problem and pain hooks

- **Problem identification and solution:** State the specific pain point your audience experiences, then introduce the product as the fix. Formula: "[If you / Stop scrolling if] you [specific pain]," then offer what fixes it. It works because viewers who have that exact problem recognise themselves and stop to see the solution. [L0160.002]
  - "Stop scrolling if you're tired of planners you never actually use."
  - "If you waste 30 minutes every morning choosing an outfit, this changes everything."
  [L0160.002]
- **Problem-first hook formula:** Name the viewer's exact problem in the first sentence, using the words the target customer uses. Add "this is for you" or an equivalent so the right person keeps watching. The viewer identifies with the problem within a second and stops scrolling. [L0392.004]
  - "If your kitchen floor is covered in crumbs every single morning, then this is for you."
  - "If your car smells like wet dog every time you drive, then this is for you."
  [L0392.004]
- **Problem-first, product as direct fix:** Name the customer's everyday problem in the first line, then present the product as the direct fix. The viewer recognises their situation and understands the benefit at once. [L0562.020]
  - "Tired of cold feet at your desk? Our heated foot warmer keeps them toasty all day."
  - "Sick of your car windows freezing at 7 am? This quick-defrost cover clears the glass in seconds."
  [L0562.020]
- **Problem plus benefit with a visible symptom:** Start with a question or statement that names a specific problem and promises a benefit for a named body area or use case, then show the product doing that job immediately. [L0657.011]
  - "Still waking up with puffy eyes? Watch this gel reduce swelling in 10 seconds."
  - "Worried about slipping on wet tile? See how these shower slippers grip the floor."
  [L0657.011]
- **Symptom-first (Source A):** Name the visible problem the buyer already notices, state what it costs them in time, money or appearance, then close with a question that invites them to recognise it. Buyers recognise symptoms faster than root causes. [L0701.042]
  - "Running shoes soaked before the first mile? Stop buying new pairs every month."
  - "Jackets stained after every commute? Your clothes deserve a fix that lasts."
  [L0701.042]
- **Problem-solution opening (Source D):** Lead with a direct question about the customer's pain ("Sick of the [specific problem]?"), then position the brand as the answer with an adjective that appeals to customer psychology, such as "wholistic", "calming" or "natural". It works because it names the problem state, triggers recognition and offers an escape path at once. [L0313.002]
  - "Tired of restless nights? This is your natural sleep solution."
  - "Frustrated with back tension? Meet your pain-free workday."
  [L0313.002]
- **Contrast question (Source D):** Open with a question or contrast that names the viewer's exact problem, then point to a different path than the one they are already on. The hook is judged by how fast it makes the viewer feel seen. [L0374.030]
  - "Are you still getting breakouts on your back after every workout? Here is the two-minute routine that finally stopped mine."
  - "If your running shoes still hurt after 5 km, don't buy another pair yet. Check this first."
  [L0374.030]
- **Frustration and "that is me" statement:** Name a frustration the target viewer already has, connect it to the product as the fix, and phrase it as a short statement that makes the viewer think "that is me". [L0764.009]
  - "Still scrubbing grease off the stovetop every night? Watch what happens in two seconds."
  - "Tired of your car smelling like wet gym bags after every rainy trip?"
  [L0764.009]
- **Specific everyday problem, number and action:** Open with one specific everyday problem the buyer already notices, state a fix with a number, then close with one action. Naming the exact situation makes the product feel relevant instead of generic. [L0794.056]
  - "Chargers dying by week three? Our braided cable is rated for 10,000 bends, so order a pack of two today."
  - "Boots soaking through on every wet walk? Our membrane liner keeps feet dry for 8 hours, so get the pair before the weekend."
  [L0794.056]
- **Relatable-problem hook:** Open with a question or statement about a problem the viewer experiences. Within seconds, show the product solving that problem on screen. Viewers who recognise themselves stay to watch. [L0795.026]
  - "Tired of wiping muddy paw prints off the floor after every walk?"
  - "Hate scrubbing burnt cheese off your pan every night?"
  [L0795.026]
- **Problem-specific creative in the customer's words:** Name the exact problem the audience has in their own words, as found in reviews, then offer the product as the fix. [L0999.045]
  - "Dog hair on your bed every morning? This brush lifts it out of wiry fur in one pass."
  - "Still stuck with cat hair on the sofa? This brush pulls it out before it spreads."
  [L0999.045]
- **Owner-group formula:** Name a specific owner group, describe the everyday annoyance they recognise, point to the visible symptom, and add a direct call to act. The viewer sees their own situation in the first line. [L0993.023]
  - "Cat owners with a sofa full of fur, this roller lifts it off in one pass."
  - "Border Collie owners whose car seats are covered in hair, this attachment cleans them in minutes."
  [L0993.023]
- **Pain-point hook:** Open with a relatable daily struggle, name the feeling it causes, then reveal the product as the fix in one sentence. [L1427.008]
  - "Dreading the wait for your kettle while you still need a second cup? Here is a quick fix that works in any mug."
  - "Tired of brewing bitter coffee that tastes flat every morning? This ready-to-use coffee gives you a smooth cup in seconds."
  [L1427.008]
- **Reassure, explain, act (Source D):** Open with a relatable pain point framed as a question, reassure the viewer that the problem is not their fault, name one mechanism of the product in plain words, and end with a simple call to action. The viewer recognises the problem first, so the product reads as a solution, not a pitch. [L1479.018]
  - "Stuck in an afternoon slump again? You're not lazy, your energy may just need support. One daily capsule helps keep focus steady."
  - "Dog still pulling on every walk? It's not you. This harness shifts pulling tension to the chest so walks feel calm."
  [L1479.018]
- **Precise customer words:** Open the hook with the exact words your target customers use to describe the problem in forums, reviews or comments. Only someone with that problem feels addressed. The reader sees their own inner voice in the first line. [L0772.018]
  - "My heel cracks every winter even after three creams, and I am sick of it."
  - "Every shirt is soaked by lunch, and nothing I have bought has fixed it."
  [L0772.018]
- **Pain-point hook over free stock footage:** Find a free stock clip that shows the frustration, convert it to grayscale, and overlay a caption that names the pain point, plus a cross mark over the clip. Viewers recognise their own problem within seconds. [L0398.011]
  - Grayscale clip of a dripping tap, caption: "Still mopping up the same puddle every morning?"
  - Grayscale clip of a cluttered desk, caption: "Losing 20 minutes a day hunting for chargers?"
  [L0398.011]
- **Warning hook:** Warn the viewer off a product, or ask them to check one detail before they act. It makes the viewer feel protected from a mistake, which holds attention longer than a plain product claim. [L1164.062]
  - "Hold off on buying [product] until you check the ingredient list on the back."
  - "Stop reordering [product] before you read the renewal terms in the checkout."
  [L1164.062]
- **Desire-result hook:** Name a result the buyer wants, then name the product or ingredient as the way to get it, in the form "if you want [result] you need [product]". The viewer sees the benefit in the first seconds. [L0901.017]
  - "If you want deeper sleep without feeling groggy, you need magnesium glycinate at night."
  - "If your knees feel stiff every morning, you need this collagen drink."
  [L0901.017]
- **Problem and relief in three seconds:** Start with the viewer's specific problem and show the relief within the first three seconds. Viewers with the same problem recognise it and keep watching, and others leave, so the ad reaches a qualified audience. [L0871.070]
  - "Tired of waking up with a stiff neck? Watch what happens after 60 seconds on this."
  - "Working from a laptop all day and feeling that back ache again? Here is the stretch that gives relief."
  [L0871.070]
- **Relief sound or reaction:** A relief sound or reaction while using the product works as a recurring hook pattern. Keep the same voice and actions across ads and change only the camera angle. [L0871.063]
- **Testimonials in the problem hook (Pain/Agitate/Solve):** In the problem description hook, use customer testimonies or direct quotes. This gives social proof at the opening, before the product enters as the solution. [L0258.026]

### Claim, benefit and transformation hooks

- **Challenge the standard, offer a better alternative:** State what people currently believe or do, then immediately introduce a different or better way. It creates doubt about the current approach and positions the product as the smarter choice. [L0160.003]
  - Formula: "Everyone says [common belief], but [your approach is better]" or "Don't [current solution], [do this instead]."
  - "Everyone says drink more water for energy, but here's what actually works."
  - "Don't buy those expensive noise-canceling headphones-try this instead for a quarter of the price."
  [L0160.003]
- **Outcome or hidden insight:** Promise a specific result or reveal a non-obvious reason, but do not explain it in the hook. Formula: "Here's [the secret / the real reason / what I discovered] about [topic]" or "How I [achieve specific result]," then pause. Curiosity and the wish to know HOW keep the viewer watching. [L0160.005]
  - "Here's the real reason your productivity hack isn't working."
  - "How I sleep 2 hours less and wake up more rested (and it's not what you think)."
  [L0160.005]
- **Transformation hook:** State that the product changed the speaker's space or health, then name the result. The viewer sees a before and after before the product is explained. A visible result creates curiosity and gives proof before any claim is made. [L0392.005]
  - "This is how my car went from covered in dust to spotless in one week."
  - "This is how a single bottle changed my morning routine and gave me back my energy."
  [L0392.005]
- **Bold claim:** Open with one specific, strong statement about the product result, so the right viewer relates at once. A direct claim filters the audience in the first second. [L0398.012]
  - "This pan fries eggs without a drop of oil."
  - "This charger refills a phone in the time it takes to make coffee."
  [L0398.012]
- **Bold claim with a payoff later:** Open with a bold claim or surprising statement that makes viewers expect a payoff, such as a shocking reveal or a question they need answered. The payoff must come later in the video, which keeps viewers to the end. [L1384.015]
  - Example A: a tiny change in the kitchen that saved a family a surprising amount each month.
  - Example B: nobody expected this result until the final second of the test.
  [L1384.015]
- **Surprising cost or loss:** Name a surprising cost or loss tied to an everyday situation, then present the product as the fix. It grabs attention with a concrete problem the viewer recognises. [L0638.033]
  - "Commuters lose hours each month to tangled cables. This organiser keeps every charger in one place."
  - "Gym goers waste money on bottles that leak. This sealed bottle stays dry in any bag."
  [L0638.033]
- **Benefit-led hook:** The hook states the target audience and problem, then creates curiosity, and the product benefit follows.
  - Ergonomic mouse: "Office workers, never ignore these three signs of wrist strain. Wrist pain often starts small, and most people only notice it when it's too late. Our curved mouse keeps your hand relaxed through an entire workday."
  - Sleep mask: "Light sleepers, never ignore these three signs of a bad night's rest. Most sleep problems start with a stray light you barely notice. Our blackout mask blocks 100% of light so you wake up rested."
  [L1425.025]
- **Budget-conscious solution:** Acknowledge the cost barrier directly, then position the product as solving both the need and the price concern. [L0160.008]
  - "Want luxury skincare without the luxury price tag? Here's how."
  - "Designer jeans energy on a thrift store budget."
  [L0160.008]
- **Daily use or essential status:** Highlight frequency or category status to show the product is proven and essential, not a trend. Daily use suggests reliability and builds confidence in real value. [L0160.007]
  - Formula: "[Number] products I [use daily / cannot live without / use every morning]" or "My must-have [product category] I use without fail."
  - "Three tools I use before 9 AM that actually change my day."
  - "The one item in my skincare routine I've used for five years straight."
  [L0160.007]
- **Authority through extensive testing:** Share your personal journey or quantify the scope of your testing (every, all, tested X number, daily, without fail). Testing builds trust, and viewers believe you have done due diligence. [L0160.004]
  - Formula: "I tried [number or scope], and here's what I kept" or "One [product] I use [frequency] is."
  - "I tested 23 coffee makers this year and kept only one."
  - "The one desk lamp I use every single workday and will never replace."
  [L0160.004]
- **Trusted source and numbered list:** A hook that credits a trusted source, such as a viral trend or a group of people, with a purchase decision adds social proof in the first seconds. A hook that promises a numbered list of reasons sets a clear, quick-to-scan promise. [L1335.053]
  - "Busy parents keep switching to this, here is why."
  - "Five reasons your kitchen needs this before the weekend."
  [L1335.053]

### Curiosity, suspense and pattern breaks

- **Suspense:** Start with a curiosity gap and delay the reveal of the product until after the first clip. Curiosity keeps people watching long enough to reach the product intro. [L0398.013]
  - "I almost threw this out before I tried it on my kitchen counter."
  - "The one thing my gym instructor never told me until I bought this."
  [L0398.013]
- **Pattern break:** Ads must interrupt what people are doing, not blend in. Short headlines of two to three words, paired with an unusual image, stop a reader mid-scroll long enough to click. The goal is a pattern break that moves attention to the offer. [L0523.032]
- **Familiar word, unexpected format:** Open by speaking directly to the target buyer and pair a familiar, high-intent product word with a format the buyer does not expect. The curiosity from the mismatch stops the scroll, and the buyer identifies with the speaker at once. [L0707.008]
  - "Sunscreen in a stick? Here is why it leaves no white cast and why my daily routine changed."
  - "Espresso-style foam in a 30-second jar? I cannot believe this replaced my morning cafe run."
  [L0707.008]
- **Unusual question or event:** Open with a specific, unusual question or event the reader cares about, then bridge to the offer as the way to understand or solve it. Curiosity holds attention long enough for the reader to reach the offer. [L1369.053]
  - "Why do some bakeries sell out by nine in the morning while the one across the street throws away its bread every night?"
  - "What is the one check that tells a warehouse manager a shipment will be late before the truck leaves the dock?"
  [L1369.053]
- **Offbeat news hook:** Find an unusual article or statistic and use it to open the ad, then link it to the product through one clear step. Keep a file of such clippings so they are ready when a product needs a surprising opening. [L1366.062, L1366.076]
  - "A survey shows that many people reuse their water bottles for days without washing them, so here is a bottle that cleans itself."
  - "A new report finds that most office chairs are sat on for more than eight hours, which is why this chair was designed around the spine."
  - "A survey finds many people reuse water bottles for days without washing them, so this bottle cleans itself."
  - "Most office chairs are sat on for over eight hours a day, which is why this one is built around the spine."
  [L1366.062, L1366.076]
- **Educational hook:** Open with a useful fact or warning that names a problem the audience cares about, then reveal the product as the solution. Viewers accept the lesson first and the sale second. [L0524.044]
  - "Three everyday habits that quietly dry out your skin and what to use instead."
  - "Two cleaning products that leave a film on your floors, and the simple swap that fixes it."
  [L0524.044]
- **Educational reveal:** Ads that reveal a problem the viewer did not know about tend to perform well, for example "did you know your dog could suffer from...". They pull the viewer into the problem. [L1425.010]
- **Question about owning the product:** Open with a question that asks the viewer to picture owning or using the product, then cut to text-to-speech listing the reasons to buy in a few sentences, and end with a short closing line. [L1383.022]
  - "Do you see yourself keeping this on your desk every morning?" followed by benefits and a closing line about the daily routine.
  - "Do you see yourself giving this as a gift this winter?" followed by reasons it suits gifting and a closing line urging a purchase.
  [L1383.022]
- **Case: "Do you see yourself needing this?":** A jewelry store used the hook "Do you see yourself needing this?" and reportedly reached about 2.5 million views with it. The speaker cited this as evidence that the hook can perform well across different products. [L1383.023]
- **Dialogue hook:** Start with an emoji of a person and a text-to-speech question such as "Why did you give me this free product?". Reply in character that the product is a gift, change the wording slightly each time, and have the other person say they would like to see more videos and ask whether they won. Finish by confirming they won. [L1383.024]
  - "Why did you give me this free bike?" answered by a gift reply and a follow-up asking whether they won.
  - "Why did you send me this free candle set?" answered by a thank-you and a question asking whether they can join the giveaway.
  [L1383.024]
- **Case: dialogue hook performance:** The dialogue hook "Why did you give me this free product?" was uploaded about three to six times before one version got traction. That version reached about 370,000 views and brought about 5,000 followers. Earlier uploads of the same format got barely any views. [L1383.025]
- **Text-story hook:** Use on-screen text that takes longer to read than the video length, for example 15 seconds of reading in a 7-second video. This forces viewers to replay, which raises average watch time, but the text must be engaging enough to keep them reading. [L1384.020]
  - Example A: a short story where the outcome is revealed only in the final frame.
  - Example B: a running dialogue where each line shows a small surprise.
  [L1384.020]
- **Story opening:** Begin with a short exchange in which someone with a real problem asks a respected person for advice. Let the answer introduce a principle that leads to the product. A concrete person and a question make the reader listen, and the answer frames the product as the practical result of wise advice. [L1369.118]
  - "A plumber with a full schedule asked his most experienced mentor how to stop losing jobs to cheaper rivals, and the answer was to sell the result the customer will see first."
  - "A new mother asked her pediatrician what matters most in a stroller, and the reply began with the one feature that parents regret not checking."
  [L1369.118]

### Audience, POV and social-proof hooks

- **Niche-targeting hook:** Address only a specific group in the first line, so non-members scroll past and members engage. Engagement from that group signals TikTok to show the video to similar users, which can give better-converting reach than a large but broad view count. [L0795.027]
  - "Every runner needs this free route tracker."
  - "Calling all home bakers: this tool fixes sticky dough in seconds."
  [L0795.027]
- **Niche hook with a cold or problem:** Name a specific audience, name the cold or problem they face in their activity, then give the product as the direct fix. The hook works because it addresses one identifiable person at the moment of the problem. [L1316.030]
  - "For every football fan at winter games: cold feet ruin the match, so wear these insulated socks all game long."
  - "For the dog walkers stuck in the rain: the waterproof jacket that keeps you dry on every walk."
  [L1316.030]
- **Hobby hook, boredom and free time:** Name the boredom at home, then show how the product changed the way the viewer spends free time. [L1426.021]
  - "Tired of scrolling every evening? Here is the one thing that filled my weekends."
  - "Your free hours deserve more than the couch. Try this build."
  [L1426.021]
- **POV hook:** Place the viewer in a first-person situation in the first second. This makes the scene feel personal and encourages them to keep watching. POV works well when the scene leads straight into a comparison or product demonstration. [L0795.038]
  - "POV: you finally find a charger that survives a full week of travel."
  - "POV: your kitchen floor stays clean after the first week with this mop."
  [L0795.038]
- **Shopping-finds hook:** Frame the product as something people discover on TikTok, Amazon or shopping feeds. This leverages curiosity about what others buy, and viewers trust products that appear socially trending. [L0398.014]
  - "The kitchen tool everyone on my feed keeps buying."
  - "Three reasons I stopped paying for the expensive version."
  [L0398.014]
- **Fear of missing out and insider knowledge:** Suggest the knowledge or product is unknown or underused, and position yourself as the one sharing the secret. FOMO triggers curiosity and urgency, and viewers do not want to be left behind. [L0160.006]
  - Formula: "Why is nobody talking about [product]," "Calling all [audience] tired of [problem]," or "If you're not [using X / doing X], you're missing out."
  - "Calling all runners tired of blisters-why isn't anyone using this?"
  - "If you're not using this app for your business, you're doing it the hard way."
  [L0160.006]
- **Follow-for-giveaway hook:** It grows followers quickly ("follow my account and I'll give you a giveaway"), but has become less effective for conversion because many sellers use the same style. Use it sparingly and do not rely on it as the main sales driver. [L0657.014]

### Copy openings (written ads and landing copy)

- **Open with "Even if...":** Start copy with "Even if..." to address the main objection the reader might have. This jugular objection, the single most common one, must be crushed first or you will lose readers. Illusory superiority means most people think they are better than average, so they assume "it might work for them but not for me". [L0196.011]
- **Mistake: skipping the jugular objection:** Not addressing the common main objection at the start of copy is a mistake. Start with "Even if..." to pre-empt what readers are thinking, especially given illusory superiority ("it might work for them, but not for me"). [L0196.063]
- **Open with customer language:** Effective ad copy opens with customer language. State their pain point directly, reference their insecurity or deepest desire, or make a bold benefit claim that resonates immediately. [L0204.004]
- **Short first sentence of body copy:** The first sentence should be very short, nearly incomplete, and easy to read, with no long or multisyllable words. Its only job is to make the reader read the second sentence. [L1366.003]
- **Headline-to-first-sentence pull (print):** Every element of a print ad (headline, subheadline, photo, caption, logo, layout) is judged by one question: does it get the reader to read the first sentence? The first body sentence should be very short, almost incomplete, with no long words. [L1366.072]
  - "Your inbox is a mess. Here is how to clear it in ten minutes."
  - "Your back hurts by noon. Four changes can stop that before lunch."
  [L1366.072]
- **Real-life scenario:** Open with the buyer inside a stressful everyday moment, describe the feelings and pressure, and only then reveal how the product resolves it. Keep technical specs for later so the scene does the emotional work first. [L1366.061, L1366.075]
  - "You are stuck in a hotel lobby, the bill is waiting, and the card reader fails; this portable terminal fixes the moment."
  - "You are on a crowded train with a phone that is about to die; this solar pack keeps you connected until you get home."
  - "The card reader fails and the line is growing behind you. This portable terminal fixes that moment."
  - "The phone is at 3 percent on a crowded train. This solar pack keeps you connected until you get home."
  [L1366.061, L1366.075]
- **Familiar scene from daily life:** Open with a scene the reader recognises, then move to the problem the product solves within the same scene. A familiar setting makes the reader picture himself, so the offer feels relevant. [L1369.054]
  - "After you finish the morning school run and drop the car keys on the counter, you still have three invoices waiting to be paid."
  - "On the first cold morning of the year, the water in the shower takes nine minutes to warm, and your kids are already late for the bus."
  [L1369.054]
- **News angle tied to the reader:** A news angle or an unusual, specific detail draws attention and can be bridged to the offer. Attention must tie to the reader's own interest in the business or life, not stand alone as a shock. [L1369.067]
- **Newsworthy first, then their affairs:** Businesspeople compete with many distractions. Give the reader something newsworthy first, then connect it to their own affairs. Once attention is diverted, bring it back by showing how the offer serves those affairs. [L1369.068]
- **Simple first line that is relevant:** The first sentence or headline must instantly say something important, valuable and useful to the reader, because an unwanted letter is treated as a pest until it proves otherwise. Gimmicks such as fake hazard warnings tend to fail. A genuinely relevant headline usually succeeds. [L1370.019]
- **Sensational shout (mistake):** A sensational shout, such as an alarming word with no link to the offer, draws the wrong response. Tie every attention-grabbing element to a reason the reader cares about the offer. [L1369.041]
- **Find the point of contact:** Use this procedure to build an opening.
  1. List the reader's dominant thoughts, such as income, family, comfort, status, promotion, business survival or a current worry.
  2. Pick the thought most closely tied to what you sell.
  3. Open with a sentence about that thought and bring in the offer as its answer.
  [L1369.042]

### On-screen text, sound and visual hooks

- **On-screen text carries much of the effect:** The on-screen text and the hook have a large share of a video's effect. The hosts estimated the text alone at about 30% of the video. A weak opening can turn a good demonstration into a low-converting video. [L0657.010]
- **Text plus unexpected background:** Combine an on-screen text hook with something happening in the background. The background element should be unexpected or slightly odd, so it catches viewers off guard and makes them curious. [L0764.007]
- **Text-to-speech or short text:** Text-to-speech in the opening can keep viewers engaged. Alternatively, show a few sentences of on-screen text with a quick transition so viewers must re-watch the video to finish reading. [L0820.043]
- **Study viral on-screen text:** Viral product videos often succeed because of their on-screen text. Study the text and structure of viral product videos and reuse the proven text pattern while filming your own product. [L1381.038]
- **On-screen hook example:** On a short product clip, the first second shows the hook text "Do you see yourself drinking this?" on screen, followed by a recreated pouring sound and a text line describing the product's benefit. [L1383.044]
- **Short, fast hooks and music:** A short, fast hook is key to TikTok creatives. Spend effort on the first seconds, the music and hook variations to find winning versions. [L1376.021]
- **Thumbnails matter less for video ads:** Feed placements often skip past thumbnails. Test the first seconds of the video (the hook) more than the thumbnail. [L0648.024]
- **Hook formats for variations:** Hook formats include a clip change, a music change, a "three reasons why" opener, a "wish I knew earlier" opener or a before-and-after opener. [L0902.017]
- **Hook scene template:** Use this template as written for the first seconds.

```
Hook, first seconds. Option one, spoken: tell viewers this is for them if [PET] hair has taken over their home. Shot: a slow pan across a living room buried in [PET] hair. Option two, spoken: say that [PRODUCT] changed their [SPACE] and gave them back their health. Shot: show the product, cut to a before view of a grimy, hair-covered [SPACE], then cut to the same [SPACE] spotless afterward.
```

  [L0392.003]

- **Hook as a pattern break in the visual:** Ads must interrupt, not blend in. The unusual image is part of the pattern break that stops the scroll. [L0523.032]

### Building hook variations

- **Variations per concept:** Write one script for the concept, then make three versions in which only the first three to five seconds change while the rest of the video stays the same. [L0902.017]
- **Keep the hook separate for testing:** The hook, meaning the first three to five seconds, decides whether viewers stay, so it must be tested separately from the rest of the video. [L0902.018]
- **One video, three tests:** Keep the video and change only the opening hook, which is one of the most important parts for grabbing attention. One video can become three test videos this way. [L1107.006]
- **Start with about six hooks:** Build a list of about six hooks and make several videos for each one. Once a hook starts performing, duplicate that video and post more variations of it. [L1383.027]
- **Hook library:** A library of about 50 hook ideas can produce around 50 variations of the same product video and supply roughly three to six months of creative. Keep the library current, because hook trends change constantly. [L0398.015]
- **Test list of 50 hooks:** A video hook test list of 50 hook ideas is recommended for TikTok-style first seconds. Use it to pick which hook goes in the first position. [L0637.056]
- **Keep notes on hooks that work:** Hooks can start with a question about the audience's issue or with a direct solution statement, and should be tested. Keep notes on hooks that work so they can be reused later, including in TikTok ads once organic results fund them. [L0795.029]

### Testing hooks

- **Test systematically:** Take a winning creative and test many hook variations until one clearly outperforms. Hook ideas should come from audience research on language, problems and context. [L0640.019]
- **Three variations of one video:** Create three variations of one video, replacing only the first 3 to 5 seconds of the clip with different openings. Run all variations inside the winning audiences. [L0648.057]
- **Lift a weak attention rate:** To raise a weak attention rate, take the video that works and place several new hooks in front of it. Make sure every hook fits the marketing angle and matches the landing page copy. Keep testing new hooks continually, even when attention is already good. [L0644.007]
- **Hook testing with the 13-pattern classification:** Use the 13-pattern set from the classification procedure to label each tested hook, so results show which pattern type performs. [L0613.012]
- **Hooks decide the click too:** A strong opening drives views beyond the hook into the click, so the hook test should track clicks as well as watch time. [L0950.040]

### Mistakes to avoid

- Spending too long before the main benefit. If the ad takes 10 seconds or more to introduce the product, demonstrate the benefit within 3 to 5 seconds, then introduce the product. [L0067.021]
- Leading with product features in the opening. Show the problem first, then the solution. [L0280.017]
- Not addressing the jugular objection at the start of copy. [L0196.063]
- Attention-grabbing content with no relation to the product, which attracts viewers who will not buy. [L0640.020]
- Delaying the product in a non-unboxing video. Unless it is a strong unboxing, show the product within the first five seconds. [L1377.021]
- Sensational shouts with no link to the offer. [L1369.041]
- Gimmicks such as fake hazard warnings, which tend to fail. [L1370.019]
- Relying on the follow-for-giveaway hook as the main sales driver. [L0657.014]
- A product introduction that takes around 10 seconds, which loses viewers before the benefit appears. [L0640.048]
